ALREADY-MITIGATED LENS — searched and found nothing in force. No trigger/policy/CHECK is relevant (this is Auth, not RLS). No app guard. No test asserts one (app/(auth)/reset-password/actions.test.ts has 11 tests; the only session-related one, line 178, asserts the OPPOSITE-direction case — that a NULL user is rejected). The only thing that exists is documentary: docs/plans/P14_FINAL_RELEASE_AUDIT.md:968 already records this as item N.6 ("/reset-password accepts any live session without re-authentication", HIGH RISK, "mitigated by enabling secure_password_change hosted"), and :1937 lists that hosted setting as an OPEN OWNER DECISION. A disclosed open decision is not a control in force, so it does not refute the finding — but it does mean this is a known, already-disclosed risk item on a release already marked RELEASE BLOCKED, not an undisclosed defect.

FRESH-ENVIRONMENT CHECK (the failure class hunted): holds. The application half is unconditional in any build (static route, guardless layout, no middleware). The GoTrue half survives any environment built from supabase/config.toml:321, which is what `supabase start` / `db reset` use — so a freshly built environment is if anything MORE exposed, not less.

ONE SUB-CLAIM I DO NOT ENDORSE (partial correction): the finding also asserts that enabling secure_password_change would break the invite->set-password flow because the app sends no reauthentication nonce. GoTrue exempts a recently-created session from the nonce requirement, which would cover the fresh invite/recovery session. I did not verify that against v2.195.0's source and did not alter the container config to test it (that would have required editing repo config and restarting a shared local service). That sub-claim should be marked unverified or dropped; it does not affect the core finding.

SEVERITY: keeping MEDIUM. The precondition is prior session compromise, which already yields full account and org-data access, so the incremental harm is persistence plus owner lockout rather than a boundary bypass — but a missing re-authentication step on password change is a standard required control, and the app's own signOut({scope:"others"}) is what performs the lockout.

title: /auth/callback silently establishes an attacker-supplied session from the URL fragment with no identity-switch warning — the session-fixation guard added to /auth/confirm was never applied to the callback that is still live
evidence:
app/auth/callback/page.tsx:100 opens a useEffect that runs on mount and, at line 195, calls `establishSessionAction(accessToken, refreshToken)` with values read straight out of `window.location.hash` — no user interaction, no confirmation, and no check of who the browser is currently signed in as. On success it calls `router.replace(next)` at line 235. app/auth/callback/actions.ts's establishSessionAction passes them to `supabase.auth.setSession()` on the SERVER client, which writes real Set-Cookie headers the browser cannot refuse (that is the documented point of doing it server-side).

Contrast app/auth/confirm/page.tsx, which for exactly this risk renders: "You are currently signed in as {user.email}. Continuing will sign you out of this browser and sign you in as the account this link was sent to." and requires an explicit Continue press. /auth/callback has neither. It is not legacy: app/(auth)/actions.ts's signUpAction sets `emailRedirectTo: ${origin}/auth/callback?next=/onboarding` and app/(auth)/forgot-password/actions.ts sets `${origin}/auth/callback?next=/reset-password`.
exploit: Attacker signs in as themselves, captures their own access_token/refresh_token, and sends the victim `https://<app>/auth/callback#access_token=<attacker>&refresh_token=<attacker>`. On load the page silently calls establishSessionAction, the server writes the attacker's session into the victim's httpOnly cookies, and router.replace sends the victim to /accept-invitation (the default) or to any same-origin path the attacker put in ?next=. The victim now browses the product as the attacker with no visible transition.
impact: Classic login CSRF / session fixation. Whatever the victim does next — creating shipments, entering emissions figures, uploading evidence PDFs — lands in the attacker's organization, where the attacker can read it. It also positions the victim to enter data on a screen the attacker controls the contents of. The redirect itself cannot leave the origin (isSafeRedirectPath holds, see attempts), so this is confined to the real product origin, which is what makes it credible rather than obvious.
freshEnvironment: Yes — this is pure client/server route code with no database, grant, seed or configuration dependency. It is present in any build of this commit.

verdicts.reasoning:
I tried to refute this on the REACHABILITY lens and failed at every step. Verified independently:

1. ROUTE EXISTS AND AUTO-RUNS. app/auth/callback/page.tsx:100 `useEffect(() => {...}, [router, searchParams])` — a mount effect, no gate. Lines 172-199: when there is no `?code=`, it reads `window.location.hash` (line 174-179), pulls `access_token` (181-184) and `refresh_token` (186-189), and if both are present calls `establishSessionAction(accessToken, refreshToken)` at line 195-198. There is no `getUser()`, no comparison against the current session, no form, no click. On success it calls `router.replace(next)` at line 235. I read the whole file; nothing else gates it.

2. THE SERVER ACTUALLY WRITES THE COOKIE. app/auth/callback/actions.ts:48-62 calls `supabase.auth.setSession({access_token, refresh_token})` on `getServerSupabaseClient()`. I read the installed library: node_modules/.pnpm/@supabase+auth-js@2.112.4/.../GoTrueClient.js `_setSession` (line 3024) decodes the JWT, and on the not-expired branch calls `_getUser(access_token)` then `await this._saveSession(session)` — it validates the token belongs to *someone*, never that it belongs to the *current* someone. src/infrastructure/supabase/server-client.ts:83-110 routes that save through next/headers `cookieStore.set` with `httpOnly: true`, i.e. real Set-Cookie headers. The repo's own comment at actions.ts:31-46 says this server-side placement was chosen precisely because "A Server Action's cookie mutations become real Set-Cookie response headers, which the browser cannot refuse."

3. NOTHING INTERCEPTS THE ROUTE. There is no middleware.ts anywhere in the repo (`find -maxdepth 2 -name middleware.ts` → empty). proxy.ts matches `/((?!_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico).*)` but its body only calls `await supabase.auth.getUser()` and returns the response (proxy.ts:118-121) — no route guard, no auth redirect.

4. THE CONTRAST IS REAL. app/auth/confirm/page.tsx:105-111 calls `supabase.auth.getUser()` and renders at 147-158: "You are currently signed in as {user.email}. Continuing will sign you out of this browser..." behind an explicit `ConfirmLinkForm` Continue press. /auth/callback has no equivalent.

5. NOT LEGACY. Three live callers confirmed in the working tree: app/(auth)/actions.ts:268 `emailRedirectTo: ${origin}/auth/callback?next=/onboarding`; app/(auth)/forgot-password/actions.ts:121 `redirectTo: ${origin}/auth/callback?next=/reset-password`; app/team/actions.ts:645 `redirectTo: ${origin}/auth/callback?next=/accept-invitation`.

6. THE CODEBASE ALREADY DOCUMENTS THE SESSION-INJECTION HALF AS REAL AND ONLY CLOSED THE OTHER HALF. app/auth/callback/is-safe-redirect-path.ts:6-11 (P13, "confirmed live"): "...sends the victim's browser to a different origin immediately after setSession() has already written the attacker's own session into the victim's cookies (session fixation)." That fix constrained `next` to a same-origin path; it left the unconditional session write in place. I re-read isSafeRedirectPath and agree the redirect cannot leave the origin, which bounds but does not remove the issue.

7. THE GUARD WAS ADDED IN THIS BRANCH AND SKIPPED THIS ROUTE. `git log --oneline -- app/auth/confirm/page.tsx` → one commit, 9766997, whose message says "/auth/confirm warns before an identity switch. A link for a different account opened in a signed-in browser is otherwise indistinguishable to the user until their data lands in the wrong organization." Its companion test tests/architecture/auth-confirm-get-is-inert.test.ts:117-131 only asserts that app/auth/callback/page.tsx does not contain "verifyOtp", with the rationale "If a second call site appears, it needs its own review of whether it is reachable by GET." `establishSessionAction` IS reachable by GET (mount effect) and never got that review.

REFUTATION ATTEMPTS THAT FAILED: no middleware gate; no `type` check (the parsed `kind` at page.tsx:201-207 feeds error copy only, never gates the call); setSession does not reject an identity switch; Next.js Server Action origin/CSRF checking does not apply because the action is invoked from the app's own page at the app's own origin; and the attacker's token acquisition is trivial (any user's own sign-in response body carries access_token/refresh_token, and the invite/magic-link flow hands the attacker exactly this URL shape for their own account).

NOT RE-RUN LIVE: no dev server was running (`curl localhost:3000/auth/callback` → 000) and I did not create auth users to avoid mutating the shared local DB, so I did not observe the Set-Cookie in a real browser. That single step is instead evidenced by the repo's own live-confirmed comment at app/auth/callback/actions.ts:31-46, written when the team moved this call server-side for exactly that effect. The fresh-environment claim holds: this is route code with no grant, seed, migration or config dependency.

Severity: MEDIUM is right. It needs the victim to open an attacker-crafted link, and the redirect is origin-confined — but the outcome is the victim silently operating as the attacker's identity, so shipments, emissions figures and uploaded evidence land in the attacker's organization.

I re-ran every cited piece of evidence against the actual files. All of it holds, and I could not find any control that stops the flow.

CITATIONS VERIFIED EXACTLY:
- app/auth/callback/page.tsx:100 — `useEffect(` opens on line 100, running on mount, deps `[router, searchParams]` (line 250). No user interaction gate.
- app/auth/callback/page.tsx:195 — `return establishSessionAction(accessToken, refreshToken);`, where accessToken/refreshToken come from lines 181-189 reading `new URLSearchParams(window.location.hash.replace(/^#/, ""))`. Straight out of the fragment, as claimed.
- app/auth/callback/page.tsx:235 — `router.replace(next)` on `result.status !== "error"`. Confirmed.
- app/auth/callback/actions.ts:48-62 — `establishSessionAction` calls `getServerSupabaseClient()` then `supabase.auth.setSession({access_token, refresh_token})`. No `getUser()`, no current-identity check, no CSRF token, no origin check beyond Next's built-in (which does not apply, since the app's own page invokes the action).

CONTRAST VERIFIED VERBATIM: app/auth/confirm/page.tsx:104-111 does `await supabase.auth.getUser()` with the comment "so the page can warn before an identity switch rather than after it", and lines 151-158 render exactly the quoted text: "You are currently signed in as {user.email}. Continuing will sign you out of this browser and sign you in as the account this link was sent to." Line 147: "Never a silent identity switch." That guard exists only in /auth/confirm.

"NOT LEGACY" VERIFIED — and it is broader than the finding claimed. grep for `auth/callback` as a redirect target returns THREE live producers, not two:
- app/(auth)/actions.ts:268 — `emailRedirectTo: ${origin}/auth/callback?next=/onboarding`
- app/(auth)/forgot-password/actions.ts:121 — `redirectTo: ${origin}/auth/callback?next=/reset-password`
- app/team/actions.ts:645 — `redirectTo: ${origin}/auth/callback?next=/accept-invitation`

REFUTATION ATTEMPTS THAT ALL FAILED:
1. Middleware guard. There is no middleware.ts; this Next version uses proxy.ts. I read all 134 lines: it only calls `supabase.auth.getUser()` (line 121) to refresh the cookie and returns `response`. It performs zero route guarding or redirection, and its matcher (line 132) covers /auth/callback. Nothing blocks a signed-in or signed-out victim from loading the page.
2. An early bail on the crafted URL. parse-auth-link-error.ts:38-48 returns null unless `error_code` or `error` is present. A crafted `#access_token=...&refresh_token=...` has neither, so `linkError` is null and execution falls through to the establishSession branch. Nothing stops it.
3. A guard inside the server client. grep of src/infrastructure/supabase/server-client.ts for getUser/setSession/throw shows only the env-var throw at line 42 and httpOnly cookie config at line 83. No identity check.
4. A test encoding a deliberate decision to omit the warning. grep of app/auth/callback/actions.test.ts for "signed in|identity|getUser|warn" returns nothing.

THE CODEBASE ITSELF CORROBORATES THE MECHANISM. app/auth/callback/is-safe-redirect-path.ts:6-11 describes the P13 finding as an attacker-controlled `next` that "sends the victim's browser to a different origin immediately after setSession() has already written the attacker's own session into the victim's cookies (session fixation)." So the session-injection half was already recognized in P13; only the redirect half was fixed. And app/auth/callback/actions.ts:42-46 states the server-side setSession was chosen precisely because "A Server Action's cookie mutations become real Set-Cookie response headers, which the browser cannot refuse the way it refuses a script write" — the exact property the finding relies on.

SCOPE NOTE (the finding got this right and did not overclaim): the PKCE `?code=` branch at page.tsx:169 is NOT exploitable this way, because exchangeCodeForSession requires the matching code_verifier cookie in the victim's own browser. Only the hash-fragment branch (lines 172-199) is. The finding also correctly limited impact by noting isSafeRedirectPath confines the redirect to the origin.

No database, grant, seed or config dependency — this is pure route code, so the fresh-environment claim holds trivially. Severity MEDIUM is fair: it requires the victim to click an attacker-crafted link (a phishing precondition), and it does not compromise the victim's own credentials; but the transition is silent on a trusted origin and lands the victim's subsequent shipment/emissions/evidence entries in the attacker's organization.

I re-read the code rather than trusting the finding, and searched for a mitigation in middleware, config, tests and later commits. I found none.

CODE FACTS CONFIRMED (my own reading):
- app/auth/callback/page.tsx:100 `useEffect(() => {` runs on mount. Lines 172-199: it reads `window.location.hash`, pulls `access_token` (181-184) and `refresh_token` (186-189), and at line 195 calls `establishSessionAction(accessToken, refreshToken)`. There is no `getUser()`, no signed-in check, no form, no click. Line 235 `router.replace(next)` on success. The only text ever rendered on the happy path is "Signing you in…" (line 268).
- app/auth/callback/actions.ts:48-80 `establishSessionAction` is `"use server"` (line 1) and calls `supabase.auth.setSession({access_token, refresh_token})` on `getServerSupabaseClient()` (53-62).
- src/infrastructure/supabase/server-client.ts:80-83 sets `cookieOptions: {secure: NODE_ENV==="production", httpOnly: true}` and 89-107 `setAll` writes via `next/headers` `cookieStore.set`. In a Server Action those become real Set-Cookie headers. So the attacker's tokens land in the victim's httpOnly session cookies exactly as claimed.
- app/auth/confirm/page.tsx:146-159 is the contrasting guard: `{user ? (...)"You are currently signed in as {user.email}. Continuing will sign you out of this browser and sign you in as the account this link was sent to."` behind `ConfirmLinkForm`'s explicit Continue. Nothing equivalent exists in the callback.

MITIGATION SEARCH (came up empty):
- `find . -maxdepth 2 -name middleware.ts -not -path ./node_modules/*` returns nothing — there is no middleware gating /auth/callback.
- next.config.ts has no `redirects()`/`rewrites()` touching the route (grep for redirects/rewrites/callback: only `headers()` and comments).
- app/auth/callback/ contains only page.tsx, actions.ts, is-safe-redirect-path.ts, parse-auth-link-error.ts and their tests — no identity-switch guard, and no test asserting one.
- tests/architecture/auth-confirm-get-is-inert.test.ts:116-131 does read the callback file, but only asserts it does NOT contain `verifyOtp`. Not a mitigation.
- The only prior hardening here is is-safe-redirect-path.ts:1-53, whose own doc comment names "session fixation" — but it only constrains `next`. It confines where the victim is sent; it does nothing about the session injection itself. So the P13 fix explicitly stopped short of this.
- git log for the two pages shows the confirm-page guard arrived in 9766997 ("make email links survive being opened by something other than the recipient") and was never back-ported to the callback.

ONE CORRECTION TO THE FINDING'S EVIDENCE. Its "It is not legacy" argument is wrong on the mechanism it cites. supabase/config.toml:352-366 wires four custom templates, and all four hardcode the destination: supabase/templates/invite.html:22, confirmation.html:4, recovery.html:14, magic_link.html:16 all point at `{{ .SiteURL }}/auth/confirm?token_hash=...`. GoTrue's `.RedirectTo` is never interpolated, so the `emailRedirectTo: ${origin}/auth/callback?next=/onboarding` at app/(auth)/actions.ts:268, the `${origin}/auth/callback?next=/reset-password` at app/(auth)/forgot-password/actions.ts:121 and the `${origin}/auth/callback?next=/accept-invitation` at app/team/actions.ts:645 no longer determine where a real user lands. No legitimate email now reaches /auth/callback.

That does NOT mitigate the defect — it arguably sharpens it. The route is still built and publicly served; the exploit never needed an email, since the attacker composes `https://<app>/auth/callback#access_token=…&refresh_token=…` himself. What it means is that /auth/callback is now dead legitimate surface that still silently establishes a session, so the correct fix is plausibly deletion (plus the two `?code=`/hash producers) rather than adding a warning. It also means any user who ever lands there is, by construction, attacker-driven.

NOT LIVE-EXECUTED: I did not stand up the app and run the exploit in a browser, so the end-to-end chain is confirmed by code reading, not by observed Set-Cookie. Every link in that chain is nonetheless explicit in the source, including the doc comment at app/auth/callback/actions.ts:38-46 which states the server-side setSession was chosen precisely because "the browser cannot refuse" the resulting cookie write. No database dependency, so the fresh-environment claim holds.

Severity MEDIUM stands: requires the victim to open an attacker link, is confined to the product origin by isSafeRedirectPath, but results in the victim transparently operating inside the attacker's organization.

title: An org admin can mint an invitation that never expires — the INSERT policy constrains org, inviter and status but not expires_at, so the 7-day window the P11 review relied on is client-controllable
exploit: An ADMIN or OWNER (their session's anon key and JWT are all that is needed — this goes through PostgREST directly, not the product's invite form, which never sets the column) inserts an invitation with expires_at far in the future. Combined with the offboarding finding above, this converts a departing admin's planted ADMIN invitation from a 7-day window into a permanent one; and organization_invitations_select_own_email's `expires_at > now()` guard, which exists to stop a lapsed invitation disclosing the org to whoever later controls that mailbox, never fires.
impact: Own-tenant, admin-privileged, and reachable only via the raw REST API rather than the UI — but it defeats two controls the security review explicitly relied on (the read-time disclosure window and the bounded acceptance window), and it is the difference between a week-long and an unbounded backdoor when chained with the un-revoked-invitation finding.
freshEnvironment: Yes. The policy text is what the migration creates; I read it back from the live catalog (pg_policy) and it matches the migration source, and the probe built its own org/membership/invitation inside a transaction so it does not depend on any pre-existing row.

verdicts.reasoning:
I could not refute this. I re-verified every link of the chain myself.

1. POLICY TEXT (source). supabase/migrations/20260828130000_organization_invitations.sql, organization_invitations_insert_admin_or_owner: `with check (app.user_is_admin_or_owner_of(org_id) and invited_by = auth.uid() and status = 'PENDING')`. No expires_at clause. I read every migration that touches organization_invitations (grep -rln gave 8 files: ...828130000, 828140000, 829260000, 829300000, 829330000, 829360000, 829380000, 829390000). None ever redefines the INSERT policy. 20260829380000 drops+recreates only the two SELECT policies (adding `expires_at > now()`) and the accept RPC; 20260829390000 does the sharing_grants mirror. So the INSERT side is never bounded.

2. POLICY TEXT (live catalog), two independently built databases. The shared local `postgres` DB was empty/mid-reset by another agent during my run (`select count(*) from pg_tables where schemaname='public'` = 0), so I used throwaway DBs in the same cluster. In `advrev_refute` and in `advrev_expiry_refute`, `select polname||' | cmd='||polcmd::text||' | CHECK='||coalesce(pg_get_expr(polwithcheck,polrelid),'-') from pg_policy where polrelid='public.organization_invitations'::regclass` returned, identically in both:
  organization_invitations_insert_admin_or_owner | cmd=a | CHECK=(app.user_is_admin_or_owner_of(org_id) AND (invited_by = auth.uid()) AND (status = 'PENDING'::text))
  organization_invitations_select_own_email | cmd=r | USING=((status = 'PENDING') AND (expires_at > now()) AND (lower(email) = lower(COALESCE(app.user_confirmed_email(), ''))))
This matches the migration source exactly, so it is a property of the schema, not of any one run.

3. NO OTHER BOUND. expires_at's only constraint is the column DEFAULT `(now() + '7 days'::interval)` (information_schema.columns). pg_constraint on the table lists only role/status/email-format checks, PK and 3 FKs — no expires_at CHECK. pg_trigger (not tgisinternal) on the table: empty. No sweeper job flips PENDING to EXPIRED; only accept_organization_invitation() does it lazily, and app/team/pending-invitations-list.tsx:50 says so explicitly ("organization_invitations has no EXPIRED status -- a row sits at PENDING until an acceptance attempt flips it").

4. MY OWN LIVE REPRODUCTION, real BEGIN...ROLLBACK, state verified before and after (db advrev_expiry_refute, which carries the seed's grants):
  begin;
  insert into auth.users(id,email,email_confirmed_at) values ('16e2b5a7-...',...);
  insert into public.organizations(id,name,slug,capabilities) values ('aaaaaaaa-0000-0000-0000-000000000002','OPUS Probe Org','opus-probe-org','{IMPORTER_DECLARANT}');
  insert into public.memberships(org_id,user_id,role) values (...,'OWNER');
  set local role authenticated; set local request.jwt.claims='{"sub":"16e2b5a7-f8c7-4935-95df-676d95454b94","role":"authenticated","email":"attacker@example.com"}';
  insert into public.organization_invitations(org_id,email,role,status,invited_by,expires_at) values (...,'victim@example.com','ADMIN','PENDING',..., timestamptz '2999-01-01') returning ...;
Output: e53fdebf-5d8e-4ddb-8aa1-e42b99b48b4c | victim@example.com | ADMIN | PENDING | 2999-01-01 00:00:00+00. After `rollback`: POST-ROLLBACK invitations = 0, orgs = 0, users = 0. Nothing committed.

5. REACHABILITY LENS (the one I was asked to apply) — the chain is complete, not hypothetical:
  - supabase/config.toml [api] `schemas = ["public", "graphql_public"]` — the table is PostgREST-exposed.
  - src/infrastructure/supabase/browser-client.ts uses NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY, "inlined into the client bundle by Next.js at build time" — the key and the user's own session JWT are both in the admin's browser.
  - `authenticated` holds table-wide INSERT: information_schema.role_table_grants for organization_invitations/grantee=authenticated returned INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE, REFERENCES, TRIGGER; information_schema.column_privileges for anon+authenticated returned 80 rows (10 columns x 8 privileges) — no column-level restriction on expires_at.
  - src/application/organizations/invitations.ts:83-97 shows the sanctioned path is a plain user-scoped `.from("organization_invitations").insert({org_id,email,role,invited_by})` through that same client. The exploit is that same request with one extra JSON key. No capability nobody has, no route that does not exist.

6. FRESH-ENVIRONMENT CHECK (the failure class I was told to hunt). It holds. supabase/seed.sql:21 `grant all on all tables in schema public to anon, authenticated, service_role;` plus :25-27 `alter default privileges ... grant all on tables` is what makes INSERT reachable locally, and seed.sql's own header says this replicates the hosted platform's provisioning bootstrap. The seed's deliberate re-revokes cover only calculation_results, record_calculation_result and TRUNCATE — nothing narrows organization_invitations. And unlike the section-19 case, this gap does not depend on grants at all: it is a missing predicate in the RLS WITH CHECK, which is created identically by the migration in every environment.

7. WHAT THE CONTROL WAS FOR. 20260829380000's header calls the read-time expiry a security fix (P11 finding #4/N2): a lapsed invitation "still discloses the target org's name/id/role indefinitely to anyone who later controls that mailbox... the exact 'mailbox reassignment' scenario". With expires_at set to 2999, `expires_at > now()` in organization_invitations_select_own_email and organizations_select_via_pending_invitation never fires, and accept_organization_invitation's `if v_invite.expires_at < now()` branch never fires. Both controls are nullified by a client-supplied column. No test asserts the bound (grep for expires_at in tests/ filtered to invitations: no hits).

WHY I LOWERED THE SEVERITY. Two real mitigations the finding under-weights. (a) The actor must already be ADMIN/OWNER of the org, and can already mint an ADMIN invitation through the UI; the delta is only the window's length, not the privilege. (b) It is not stealthy: organization_invitations_select_admin_or_owner lets every remaining ADMIN/OWNER read the row, app/team/pending-invitations-list.tsx renders "Awaiting acceptance - expires {date}" so it displays as "expires 1 January 2999", the UPDATE policy lets any admin revoke it at any time, and invitations.ts:120-155 now writes a membership.invitation_created audit event. That makes this a hardening gap in a control the project itself codified, rather than a privilege-boundary break — LOW, not MEDIUM. The fix is one clause (`and expires_at <= now() + interval '7 days'`, or dropping the column from the insertable set), and it is worth making because the project explicitly relies on that window twice.

CAVEAT, stated rather than buried: because the shared local postgres DB was being reset by another agent throughout my run, my probes ran against throwaway DBs in the same cluster whose auth schema is a 5-column shim (id, email, email_confirmed_at, raw_user_meta_data, created_at), not real Supabase auth. That does not affect this finding — the INSERT policy reads only app.user_is_admin_or_owner_of(org_id), auth.uid() and status — but I did not exercise the acceptance side end-to-end against a real auth.users, so the "unbounded acceptance window" half of the impact is argued from the RPC source (the `if v_invite.expires_at < now()` branch) rather than executed.

- Column default only: `expires_at | (now() + '7 days'::interval) | NO` (information_schema.columns) — a DEFAULT, overridable by any client supplying the column.
- Later migrations: `grep -rn organization_invitations supabase/migrations/` — the only later change to these policies is 20260829380000, which re-creates organization_invitations_select_own_email (adding `expires_at > now()` and app.user_confirmed_email()); it never touches the INSERT policy. 20260903130000 only adds two audit event types. - Column-level grants: after seed.sql, `authenticated` holds DELETE,INSERT,REFERENCES,SELECT,TRIGGER,UPDATE on the table with no column list, so expires_at is writable. (Before the seed it held only REFERENCES/TRIGGER — i.e. the exploit precondition is created by the documented seed step, which strengthens rather than weakens the fresh-environment claim.)

title: The certification run's secret scan is inert, and the audit document cites its vacuous output as a passing gate while explicitly asserting it was verified
evidence: .github/workflows/ci.yml:602 uses "$KNOWN_SAFE_PROCESS_ENV_ASSIGNMENT", which is never assigned anywhere in the file (`grep -n KNOWN_SAFE .github/workflows/ci.yml` returns only KNOWN_SAFE_LOCAL_DEMO_JWT at :562, KNOWN_SAFE_LOCAL_PG_URL at :570, and the three uses at :600-602). The step opens with `set -euo pipefail` (:499) and the expansion sits inside `MATCHES="$(printf ... | grep -vE "$UNDEF" || true)"` (:599-602), so the unbound-variable error kills the substitution and `|| true` swallows it, leaving MATCHES empty unconditionally; `if [ -n "$MATCHES" ]` (:604) can therefore never fire and :610 always prints the success string. Proven three ways. (1) Mechanism, reproduced: `bash -c 'set -euo pipefail; M="$(printf "a\n" | grep -vE "$UNDEF_VAR" || true)"; echo exit=$? matches=[$M]'` -> `bash: line 5: UNDEF_VAR: unbound variable` / `exit=0 matches=[]`. (2) End to end, against planted secrets: I built a throwaway git repo containing `SUPABASE_DB_PASSWORD=hunter2secretvalue` and `const k = "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9abcdefghijklmnop";`, ran the exact step body copied from ci.yml, and got `RAW_MATCHES=[leak.env:1:SUPABASE_DB_PASSWORD=hunter2secretvalue / leak2.ts:1:const k = "eyJ...";]` then `scan.sh: line 17: KNOWN_SAFE_PROCESS_ENV_ASSIGNMENT: unbound variable` then `No secret-shaped literals found in tracked files.` with STEP EXIT=0. (3) In the real certification run itself: `gh run view 33742947242 --log` line 1909 = `/home/runner/work/_temp/7c8f5edd-...sh: line 104: KNOWN_SAFE_PROCESS_ENV_ASSIGNMENT: unbound variable`, line 1911 = `No secret-shaped literals found in tracked files.` The same pair appears in run 33743652237 (branch head 0679e60). `git show 464d6d8 -- .github/workflows/ci.yml` shows the commit added only the `| grep -vE "$KNOWN_SAFE_PROCESS_ENV_ASSIGNMENT"` line and no definition.
exploit: Commit any file containing a dotenv-style `SUPABASE_DB_PASSWORD=<real password>` or a service-role JWT and push. The build-and-test 'Scan for committed secrets' step reports clean and exits 0 regardless. The fast-gates job's separate, simpler scan (ci.yml:112) does not carry the SUPABASE_(SERVICE_ROLE_KEY|DB_PASSWORD|ANON_KEY)= or postgres(ql):// patterns at all — I confirmed it reports `Secret scan clean.` on a repo whose only tracked file is `SUPABASE_DB_PASSWORD=hunter2secretvalue` — so neither job catches that class any more. Separately, running the filter the document says was committed (`process\.env\.SUPABASE_[A-Z_]+ = [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*;`) over the tree at HEAD produces three matches in docs/plans/P14_FINAL_RELEASE_AUDIT.md itself (lines 2384, 2389, 2505 — the prose containing `SUPABASE_DB_PASSWORD=hunter2secret`), i.e. the described fix would fail CI on this very document. The gate passes only because it is dead.
impact: The audit document presents this as an executed certification gate. §22 F's table lists 'Secret scan | `No secret-shaped literals found in tracked files.`' as evidence in the passing run. §22 D asserts of this exact change: 'Verified both directions: the two real lines clear, that dotenv line still flagged.' §22 G, in the section that tells the reviewer where to look, says: 'the secret-scan filter is anchored on `process.env.` and a trailing semicolon, so a dotenv-style `SUPABASE_DB_PASSWORD=hunter2secret` is **still flagged** — checked explicitly.' Neither statement can be true: the filter regex was never committed. Commit 464d6d8's message makes the same false claim ('Verified both directions before committing'). This is the document's own flagged pattern — 'the agent adjusted the gate and the gate then passed' — realised in the worst form: the gate was not adjusted, it was disabled, and the reader is specifically reassured it was not. No secret is currently committed (I ran the intended pattern manually over the tree; the only hits are the two known process.env assignments in tests/integration/calculation-reproduction.test.ts:274,462 and the audit document's own prose), so the harm today is a permanently vacuous release gate plus a false certification claim, not a live credential leak.
freshEnvironment: Yes, and it is worse in a fresh environment: the defect lives in the committed .github/workflows/ci.yml at branch head 0679e60 (verified present at 464d6d8, a977e72 and 0679e60 via `git show <sha>:.github/workflows/ci.yml | grep -n KNOWN_SAFE_PROCESS_ENV_ASSIGNMENT`), so every future CI run on any clean runner reproduces it. I confirmed it in two independent GitHub-hosted runs (33742947242 and 33743652237), each on a fresh runner, not on this machine.

title: seed.sql does not restore the 'final intended posture' it and the runbook claim: seven SECURITY DEFINER RPCs are anon-executable in every freshly built environment, and the new posture comparator passes on it
evidence: supabase/seed.sql:23 `grant all on all functions in schema public to anon, authenticated, service_role;` and :31-32 `alter default privileges in schema public grant all on functions to anon, authenticated, service_role;` run after every migration. The compensating block (:83-101) re-asserts the narrowing for `record_calculation_result` only; :104-110 re-assert the TRUNCATE revoke. Nothing re-asserts the other seven. Live, on the app's local Postgres: `select p.proname, p.proacl::text from pg_proc p join pg_namespace n on n.oid=p.pronamespace where n.nspname='public'` returns `accept_organization_invitation|{postgres=X/postgres,authenticated=X/postgres,anon=X/postgres,service_role=X/postgres}` and the same `anon=X/postgres` for accept_sharing_grant_invitation, create_organization_with_owner, list_org_members, record_declaration_filed, record_shared_data_consumption and sharing_counterparty_org_names — while record_calculation_result is correctly `{postgres=X/postgres,service_role=X/postgres}`. No migration ever grants anything to anon: `grep -rn -i 'to anon' supabase/migrations/*.sql` returns two comment lines and no statement; the migrations do `revoke all on function public.X from public; grant execute on function public.X to authenticated;` (e.g. 20260829330000_p9_declarations_schema.sql:1030-1031, 20260828130000_organization_invitations.sql:302-303). Mechanism proven in a throwaway database (created and dropped): after `revoke all on function public.pretend_rpc() from public; grant execute ... to authenticated;` -> `after_migration anon=false`; after replaying seed.sql's grant block and its compensating revokes -> `after_seed anon=true`, acl `{postgres=X/postgres,authenticated=X/postgres,anon=X/postgres,service_role=X/postgres}`. The default ACL the seed installs also affects future functions: inside `begin ... rollback`, `create function public.zz_future_rpc() ... security definer` yields `freshly created function anon exec = true`. And `node scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs --check postgresql://postgres:postgres@127.0.0.1:54322/postgres` on this database prints all nine self-checks `[OK]` and `RESULT: POSTURE MATCHES`.
exploit: NONE reachable today — this is a defence-in-depth and documentation defect, and I say so rather than overstate it. I probed it: as role anon, `select count(*) from public.sharing_counterparty_org_names()` returns 0 and `select * from public.list_org_members('00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000')` raises 'Not a member of this organization.'; the other five begin with `if auth.uid() is null then raise exception`. The structural exposure is that any future public function — including the next SECURITY DEFINER RPC a migration adds — is EXECUTE-granted to anon and authenticated by the default ACL, and a migration's `revoke all ... from public` does not remove a role-specific grant.
impact: The claim is what is defective. §22 B states seed.sql 'now states the final intended posture rather than only the bootstrap', and docs/runbooks/DEPLOYMENT.md:566-569 repeats it verbatim in the fresh-project rebuild — the documented recovery path — adding only 'If a future migration adds another revoke-based control, it has to be added there too.' A reader of the recovery runbook is told the posture is restored; it is restored for three controls out of ten. §22 also generalises the lesson correctly ('any blanket grant that runs after a narrow revoke undoes it') and then does not apply it to the seven function grants sitting in the same file. Compounding it, DEPLOYMENT.md:571-578 nominates `compare-database-posture.mjs --check` as the step-6 verification, and that tool reports POSTURE MATCHES on precisely this database — the self-check set covers TRUNCATE and INSERT policies but has no function-grant assertion, so the acceptance test written to stop vacuous passes passes vacuously here. Nothing in the audit document discloses any of this.
freshEnvironment: Yes — it is created by a fresh build, not merely present on this one. `supabase db reset`/`supabase start` runs seed.sql as the last step after all migrations, so the blanket function grant is applied after every `revoke ... from public`. I did not rely on the current database's history: I reproduced the whole mechanism from scratch in a separate database (`create database audit_seed_probe`, since dropped) using seed.sql's own statements, and separately showed the seed's default ACL grants anon EXECUTE on a function created afterwards. CI builds the same way, and CI is green.

title: The document's masthead states a head SHA and push status that are both false at the commit under review
evidence: docs/plans/P14_FINAL_RELEASE_AUDIT.md:3-7 (the unlabelled blockquote at the top of the file, before any section): 'Branch `phase14/release-hardening`, head `4aa624d`, branched from `95c95bb`. ... **Nothing has been pushed.**' Actual state at the reviewed commit: `git rev-parse HEAD` = 0679e60d6ffdaec24718c584570dcedb9637aa46, and `git branch -a -v` shows `remotes/origin/phase14/release-hardening 0679e60`, i.e. the branch is pushed. `git rev-list --count 95c95bb..4aa624d` = 17, versus 36 commits at HEAD. §§18-22 each open with a 'stands as written' disclaimer, but the masthead carries none and is the first thing a reader sees.
exploit: NONE — structural. A reader who opens the file and stops at the masthead concludes the branch is at 4aa624d and unpushed, when it is at 0679e60, pushed, and has had six CI runs.

freshEnvironment: Yes — it is committed file text at 0679e60, independent of any database or environment.

ALREADY-MITIGATED LENS — what I searched for and what I found:

title: Internal numeric contradiction in §22 on how many defects CI found, and a stale commit count carried forward as current in §20
evidence: docs/plans/P14_FINAL_RELEASE_AUDIT.md §22 A: 'Four runs, each failing further along than the last, produced six defects.' §22 G, same section: 'Three of the seven findings were fixed in `ci.yml` itself'. Six versus seven, with no reconciliation. Separately, §20 A states 'Pushing could deploy 22 unreviewed commits and 11 unapplied migrations' worth of code'; §20's own candidate SHA is e72d4988db5dc4473050c9b65019181370e440ee, and `git rev-list --count 95c95bb..e72d498` = 27, not 22. The 22 figure is correct only for 1b4a6c7 (§18 A), verified: `git rev-list --count 95c95bb..1b4a6c7` = 22.
exploit: NONE — structural.
impact: Minor, but in a document whose stated value is that its figures were each produced by a command run in that session, two figures were not re-derived when the section carrying them was written. It weakens the 'every figure below was produced by a command run in this session' framing that the masthead uses to earn the reader's trust in the harder-to-check numbers.
freshEnvironment: Yes — committed document text; checked against git history, which is environment-independent.

verdicts.reasoning:
Re-derived all three claims independently; all confirmed.

(1) §22 contradiction, both sentences inside section 22 with no reconciliation: P14_FINAL_RELEASE_AUDIT.md:2275-2276 "Four runs, each failing further along than the last, produced six defects." vs :2498-2499 "Three of the seven findings were fixed in `ci.yml` itself". I grepped lines 2261-2530 for six/seven/defect; the only other "six" is :2493 "the six owner-UAT findings", an unrelated set. No reconciling text exists.

(2) §20 stale commit count: :1584 names the candidate SHA as e72d4988db5dc4473050c9b65019181370e440ee; :1626 says "Pushing could deploy 22 unreviewed commits and 11 unapplied migrations' worth of code". My runs: `git rev-list --count 95c95bb..e72d498` = 27 (not 22); `git rev-list --count 95c95bb..1b4a6c7` = 22.

(3) Stronger corroboration than the finding claimed: the identical sentence at :514 in §18 (candidate SHA 1b4a6c7, per :448) reads "22 unreviewed commits and 9 unapplied migrations". Migration counts I ran: `git diff --name-only 95c95bb..e72d498 -- supabase/migrations | wc -l` = 11; same for 1b4a6c7 = 9. So §20 refreshed the migration figure for its own SHA and carried the commit figure forward unchanged. This also rules out a charitable reading where "22" means something other than branch commit count: §18 A:452 labels it explicitly "Commits on the branch | 22".

REACHABILITY lens: this is a documentation defect, so the actor is the independent reviewer the document addresses and the path is reading the committed file at the candidate SHA. No capability, role, RLS grant, or route is required, and the evidence is git history, hence environment-independent. The lens does not refute it.

Severity LOW is correct: no exploit, no product impact, no security or regulatory consequence. It matters only because the masthead at :8 states "Every figure below was produced by a command run in this session", and two figures in the document were not re-derived when their section was written, which weakens the framing that earns trust in the harder-to-check numbers.

CONFIRMED on my own re-derivation; every quoted string and every number checks out.

(1) Six-vs-seven, both inside §22:
- P14_FINAL_RELEASE_AUDIT.md:2275-2276 (§22 A): "Four runs, each failing further along than the last, produced six defects."
- P14_FINAL_RELEASE_AUDIT.md:2498 (§22 G): "Three of the seven findings were fixed in `ci.yml` itself"
A grep for six/seven restricted to §22 (lines 2261-2560) returns only those two, plus "Seven security tests failed in run 1" (failing tests, a different quantity) and "six of the nineteen findings require it" (owner UAT). There is no reconciling sentence. Counting the enumerated defects: §22 B = 1 (seed.sql blanket grant), §22 C = 4 Playwright fixes (the doc itself writes them as "1.", "2. and 3.", "4."), §22 D = 2 CI gaps -> 7 if C's 2 and 3 count separately, 6 if merged. Both figures are derivable, which is exactly the unreconciled contradiction the finding names. Corroborating evidence the "seven" is authoritative: the commit that introduced §22 is `0679e60 docs(p143): CI on the release candidate, and the seven things it found`, so the doc's own commit subject disagrees with §22 A's body text.

(2) Stale commit count in §20:
- P14_FINAL_RELEASE_AUDIT.md:1584: "**Candidate SHA:** `e72d4988db5dc4473050c9b65019181370e440ee`"
- P14_FINAL_RELEASE_AUDIT.md:1626: "Pushing could deploy 22 unreviewed commits and 11 unapplied migrations' worth of code"
- `git rev-list --count 95c95bb..e72d498` -> 27. Also 27 with `--no-merges` and with `--first-parent`, so no counting convention makes 22 correct for that SHA.
- `git rev-list --count 95c95bb..1b4a6c7` -> 22, and line 449 (§18) names `1b4a6c7356e96976404c8a310a82b4c294d04bed` as that pass's release candidate; line 514 carries the identical sentence with "22 unreviewed commits and 9 unapplied migrations". So §20 copied §18's sentence, updated 9 -> 11 for migrations, and left the commit count at the stale 22.
- `git log --oneline 1b4a6c7..e72d498` lists exactly 5 commits (e72d498, 06cea94, a80e94c, acdb439, eebab80); 22 + 5 = 27, confirming the arithmetic.

(3) The framing the finding says is weakened is real: line 8 of the same file reads "Every figure below was produced by a command run in this session."

Assessment: purely a documentation-accuracy defect, no product, security or regulatory effect, no exploit. LOW is the right severity rather than INFO because one of the two errors understates a risk figure inside a "do not push, this could deploy N unreviewed commits" warning in a release-gating document whose stated value is that each figure was freshly derived. Note on category: the finding is labelled AUDIT_HONESTY, but the evidence supports carelessness (a copied sentence half-updated; a body count contradicting the author's own commit subject), not deception -- the finding does not claim deception either.

I re-ran every check independently rather than trusting the finder's evidence, and applied the already-mitigated lens by grepping the whole document for any reconciling text. Both limbs confirm.

LIMB 1 — six vs seven, within §22.
`docs/plans/P14_FINAL_RELEASE_AUDIT.md:2275-2276` (§22 A): "CI had **never run on this branch**. Four runs, each failing further / along than the last, produced six defects. **None is in the product.**"
`docs/plans/P14_FINAL_RELEASE_AUDIT.md:2498-2499` (§22 G): "**One caveat the reviewer should weigh directly.** Three of the seven / findings were fixed in `ci.yml` itself..."
Both sentences describe the same set — what the P14.3 CI pass found. No reconciliation exists: `grep -n "seven|Seven"` over the file returns only four hits (167, 2175, 2291, 2498), none of which explains the mismatch; `grep -n "six defects|six findings|seven findings|seven defects"` returns only line 2276. Line 2291 is a different "seven" ("Seven security tests failed in run 1"), i.e. failing tests, not findings — so it does not reconcile the two counts, it is a third number a reader could confuse with them.

The document's own commit subject sides against §22 A: `git log --oneline 1b4a6c7..0679e60` shows the head commit is `0679e60 docs(p143): CI on the release candidate, and the seven things it found`. So the "six" in §22 A contradicts both §22 G and the commit that introduced §22.

I also tried to reconstruct which count is right and could not make "six" work from the section's own enumeration. §22 B = 1 (seed.sql), §22 C = "four fixes, all in the test" (nav click; two strict-mode assertions; missing timeout), §22 D = 2 CI gaps (secret-scan false positive; health check skipping), plus the APP_URL health-check failure discussed only in §22 G. That is 7 or 8 depending on whether the two assertions are counted as one. Six is not reachable without an unstated grouping rule. The three ci.yml fixes in §22 G do check out: `git show --stat 464d6d8 -- .github/workflows/ci.yml` = 24 insertions/1 deletion (secret-scan filter + health-check env passthrough) and `git show --stat a977e72` = 11 insertions to `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (APP_URL), i.e. three findings fixed in ci.yml.

LIMB 2 — stale commit count in §20 A.
`docs/plans/P14_FINAL_RELEASE_AUDIT.md:1626-1627` (§20 A): "**No push was made.** Pushing could deploy 22 unreviewed commits and 11 / unapplied migrations' worth of code to a system serving two real / organisations..."
§20's own candidate SHA (line ~1584): `e72d4988db5dc4473050c9b65019181370e440ee`.
Commands run:
  `git rev-list --count 95c95bb..e72d498` -> 27
  `git rev-list --count 95c95bb..1b4a6c7` -> 22
So 22 is the §18 figure (§18 A's table literally records "Commits on the branch | 22" for candidate `1b4a6c7`), carried into §20 unchanged while the section's candidate had moved five commits on. The stale-carry reading is strengthened, not weakened, by the neighbouring number: the identically-shaped sentence at line 514-515 in the earlier section reads "22 unreviewed commits and 9 unapplied migrations", so the migration count WAS re-derived for §20 (9 -> 11) and the commit count was not. Nor is 22 rescuable as a code-only count: §20 says "the code it certifies is unchanged from `06cea94`", and `95c95bb..06cea94` = 26; excluding the two docs commits in that range still gives 25.

Both are documentation-integrity defects only — no code path, no database control, no exploit. I ran no mutation probes; nothing here touches the database. Severity LOW is correct as claimed: the document's masthead (lines 8-10) stakes its credibility on "Every figure below was produced by a command run in this session", and two figures in it demonstrably were not.

title: The restore-drill acceptance gate passes on a database where the entire P14.1 output-forgery fix has been reverted
evidence:
scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs — SELF_CHECKS begins at line 252 and contains nine checks; `truncate_granted_to_api_roles` (line 402) is the only privilege check in it, and its own `why` string says 'the P14 revoke (20260903170000) must survive a restore, and a restore is exactly where a grant silently comes back'. There is no equivalent check for 20260903190000. `effective_grants` (line 123) and `function_grants` (line 169) exist but are COMPARISON checks, skipped entirely in `--check` mode (line 510: `const selfOnly = args[0] === "--check"`).

Proved live inside a real BEGIN...ROLLBACK (scratchpad/posture_blind.sql, run via psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 54322):

  BEFORE calcres write grants (anon/auth) | 0
  BEFORE rpc exec authenticated           | false
  grant insert, update, delete on public.calculation_results to anon, authenticated;
  grant execute on function public.record_calculation_result(...) to anon, authenticated;
  AFTER  calcres write grants (anon/auth) | 6
  AFTER  rpc exec authenticated           | true
  SELF auth_schema_and_helpers_present       | 0
  SELF policy_functions_resolve              | 0
  SELF tables_without_rls                    | 0
  SELF rls_without_policies                  | 0
  SELF tables_without_insert_policy          | 0
  SELF api_roles_hold_their_grants           | 0
  SELF truncate_granted_to_api_roles         | 0
  SELF security_definer_without_search_path  | 0
  ROLLBACK
  POST-ROLLBACK calcres write grants (anon/auth) | 0
  POST-ROLLBACK rpc exec authenticated           | false

Zero offending rows on every self-check means the script reaches `if (failures === 0) { console.log("RESULT: POSTURE MATCHES"); process.exit(0); }` (line 598).
exploit:
1. Restore or provision a database by any route that re-applies a broad grant after the narrow revokes — a pg_dump/pg_restore round trip (a dump records the grants that exist, never their absence), a PITR restore into a fresh project whose bootstrap re-runs the platform's `grant all on all tables/functions in schema public`, or a pre-72701dd copy of supabase/seed.sql.
2. Follow docs/runbooks/BACKUP_RESTORE.md line 530: `node scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs --check "<dsn>"` — the form the runbook prescribes 'against a restored target on its own, before a source is available', which is the only available form after a PITR restore because the source is gone.
3. The script prints RESULT: POSTURE MATCHES and exits 0 — the identical verdict string the full two-DSN comparison prints. Nothing in the log distinguishes the two.
4. The database now permits an ordinary authenticated member to INSERT a fabricated embedded_emissions_tco2e directly into calculation_results and have record_declaration_filed freeze it into an immutable filed_snapshot — the exact release blocker a80e94c fixed, reproduced at 0.001 against a true 139.
impact: The gate that certifies disaster recovery cannot see the revocation of the control that stops emissions-figure forgery reaching a filed CBAM declaration. An operator who follows the runbook exactly gets POSTURE MATCHES on a database where the P14.1 blocker is reopened. Bounded honestly: the two-DSN comparison mode DOES include effective_grants and function_grants as critical checks, so a restore compared against a still-correct source is covered; the blindness is specific to `--check` mode and to the case where the source's own posture was already re-opened. But `--check` is exactly the mode the runbook prescribes for the source-less case, and the seed.sql incident of the same day is a live demonstration that source posture does silently regress.
freshEnvironment: Yes. The gap is a property of the SELF_CHECKS array in the committed script, not of any data in this database — the array simply contains no query about INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on calculation_results or EXECUTE on record_calculation_result. My probe granted the privileges and re-ran every self-check's exact SQL inside one transaction, so the result is independent of what this database happened to hold; the post-ROLLBACK re-read confirmed the grants (6) and RPC execute (true) both returned to their original 0 / false.

verdicts.reasoning:
I could not refute the core, but I disproved a large part of the evidence and the headline claim, so the severity drops.

WHAT I CONFIRMED IN THE CODE (my own read, scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs, 614 lines):
- SELF_CHECKS runs from line 252 to 429 and holds exactly nine checks (names at lines 254, 277, 301, 314, 327, 344, 383, 402, 414). The only privilege-value assertion among them is `truncate_granted_to_api_roles` (402); `api_roles_hold_their_grants` (383) only asserts a nonzero grant count.
- `grep -n "calculation_results\|record_calculation_result" scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs` returns hits only at lines 362, 366, 371 — all inside the *exemption list* of `tables_without_insert_policy`. There is no query anywhere in SELF_CHECKS about INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on calculation_results or EXECUTE on record_calculation_result.
- `effective_grants` (123) and `function_grants` (169) are in CHECKS, not SELF_CHECKS, and main() at 510/519 skips CHECKS entirely when argv[0] === "--check". Correct as reported.
- DEPLOYMENT.md:574 prescribes `--check` for post-deploy posture verification and names `truncate_granted_to_api_roles` and `tables_without_insert_policy` as "the two checks that catch a re-granted surface" — but the second one explicitly exempts calculation_results (line 371), so it structurally cannot.

WHAT I DISPROVED (the finding's own exploit narrative is partly wrong):
1. Exploit step 4 is false. Restoring the *table* write grants does NOT let a member INSERT a forged row, because 20260903190000 also DROPs `calculation_results_insert_own_org_as_self`, and no grant restores a dropped policy. Proved live (throwaway DB opus_reach_refute, dropped afterwards):
   begin; grant insert,update,delete on public.cr to anon, authenticated; set local role authenticated; insert into public.cr (id,emissions) values (1,'0.000001'); rollback;
   -> ERROR:  new row violates row-level security policy for table "cr"
   (cr modelled the post-P14.1 state: RLS on, SELECT policy only, no INSERT policy.)
2. Every blanket-grant route the finding actually names IS caught. `grant all` on a table includes TRUNCATE, so the existing truncate self-check fires. Proved live:
   begin; grant all on all tables in schema public to anon, authenticated;
   TRUNCATE-CHECK-ROWS: 2 / INSERT-GRANTS: 2 ; rollback
   So supabase/seed.sql:21 (`grant all on all tables ...`) and a platform bootstrap `grant all on all tables/functions` both trip `truncate_granted_to_api_roles` and print POSTURE DIFFERS. The finding's probe avoided this only by hand-granting insert/update/delete without truncate — a state no operation it names produces.
3. A pg_dump/pg_restore of a correct source does not manufacture grants: the dump emits the exact ACL (`REVOKE ALL ON FUNCTION ... FROM PUBLIC; GRANT ALL ON FUNCTION ... TO service_role;`, dump lines 53-54 of my reproduction).

WHAT SURVIVES, AND WHY I CANNOT REFUTE IT: the function-EXECUTE half is real and reachable by an ordinary restore, with all nine self-checks green. Proved live with two throwaway DBs (both dropped):
  source: create function public.record_calculation_result(int); revoke all ... from public, anon, authenticated; grant execute ... to service_role;
    -> proacl = {postgres=X/postgres,service_role=X/postgres}
  target: alter default privileges for role postgres in schema public grant all on functions to postgres, anon, authenticated, service_role;   (the shape supabase's own bootstrap uses — this cluster carries exactly that entry for supabase_admin: `supabase_admin|public|f|{postgres=X,anon=X,authenticated=X,service_role=X}` in pg_default_acl, and supabase/seed.sql:31-32 sets the same for role postgres and never revokes it at the tail)
  pg_dump source | psql target ->
    proacl = {postgres=X/postgres,anon=X/postgres,authenticated=X/postgres,service_role=X/postgres}
    has_function_privilege('authenticated','public.record_calculation_result(integer)','EXECUTE') = t
    TRUNCATE self-check rows = 0  (gate stays silent)
Because `REVOKE ALL ... FROM PUBLIC` does not revoke from anon/authenticated, the target's default privileges survive the restore. record_calculation_result is SECURITY DEFINER and takes p_embedded_emissions_tco2e straight from the caller (20260903190000 lines ~300-330; the migration's own comment says "the member would simply pass the forged number to the function"), and PostgREST exposes public functions at /rest/v1/rpc/, so EXECUTE for `authenticated` does reopen forgery without needing any policy back. No SELF_CHECK looks at it.

WHY MEDIUM, NOT HIGH: this is a gap in a verification gate, not a live vulnerability — the RC's migrations and the fixed seed.sql are correct, the two-DSN mode covers it via `function_grants`/`effective_grants` (both critical), and the loudest regression routes trip the truncate proxy check. The honest defect is narrower than the title: "--check has no direct assertion for the 20260903190000 revokes, and there is a real restore path (target-side default privileges on functions) where EXECUTE on the trusted-write RPC returns to `authenticated` with every self-check green."

CAVEAT ON METHOD: I could not re-run the finding's probe against the app's own local database. At the time of my checks the local `postgres` DB held zero public tables and `supabase_migrations.schema_migrations` did not exist (`select count(*) from information_schema.tables where table_schema='public'` -> 0), i.e. it was mid/post-reset from another session. All my live evidence therefore comes from throwaway databases in the same cluster that reproduce the relevant Postgres semantics exactly; all three (opus_reach_refute, opus_src_refute, opus_tgt_refute) were dropped when I finished, and no write touched any app table or any production database.

The finding's code reading is accurate, but its exploit chain is not. Two independent halves of it fail.

WHAT I CONFIRMED (the finding's descriptive claims are true):
- scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs:252 begins SELF_CHECKS; it holds exactly nine checks, and none of them queries INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on calculation_results or EXECUTE on record_calculation_result. Verified by reading lines 252-429.
- Line numbers check out: effective_grants:123, function_grants:169, truncate_granted_to_api_roles:402, `const selfOnly = args[0] === "--check"`:510, "RESULT: POSTURE MATCHES":599 (the `if (failures === 0)` at 598).
- `--check` genuinely skips all comparison CHECKS: line 524 `if (!selfOnly) {` wraps the CHECKS loop at 529; SELF_CHECKS at 573 always runs.
- docs/runbooks/BACKUP_RESTORE.md:530 and :633 do prescribe `--check` for the source-less case.

WHERE IT BREAKS — REFUTATION 1: every restore route the finding names DOES trip an existing self-check. Its step 1 names three vectors, all of which grant TRUNCATE, and truncate_granted_to_api_roles (line 402) fires on exactly that. Proved live inside a real BEGIN...ROLLBACK on 127.0.0.1:54322:

  BEFORE truncate grants | 0
  grant all on all tables in schema public to anon, authenticated, service_role;
  AFTER privileges held by authenticated | DELETE,INSERT,REFERENCES,SELECT,TRIGGER,TRUNCATE,UPDATE
  SELFCHECK truncate_granted_to_api_roles rows | 2   <-- non-zero => RESULT: POSTURE DIFFERS, exit 1
  ROLLBACK
  POST-ROLLBACK table exists | 0

`git show 72701dd~1:supabase/seed.sql` line 21 is `grant all on all tables in schema public to anon, authenticated, service_role;` with no revokes — so the pre-72701dd seed, the platform bootstrap that seed's own comment describes, and any `grant all`-style re-provision all grant TRUNCATE and fail the gate loudly. The finding's probe granted only `insert, update, delete` — a hand-picked set that deliberately omits TRUNCATE and corresponds to no route it names. That is why its self-checks all returned 0. A pg_dump/pg_restore round trip reproduces the source ACL including its revokes (and with --no-privileges strips all grants, which api_roles_hold_their_grants at line 397 catches).

REFUTATION 2: the claimed impact ("permits an ordinary authenticated member to INSERT a fabricated embedded_emissions_tco2e directly into calculation_results") is false for a grant-only regression. Migration 20260903190000_p141_calculation_results_trusted_write_only.sql does `drop policy if exists calculation_results_insert_own_org_as_self` BEFORE the revoke. RLS-on with no INSERT policy denies the write regardless of grants; a grant cannot resurrect a policy. Proved live, same transaction:

  create table public.zz_opus_rls(...); alter table ... enable row level security;
  create policy sel ... for select to authenticated using (true);
  grant all on all tables in schema public to anon, authenticated;
  set local role authenticated; insert into public.zz_opus_rls values (1,'forged');
  ERROR:  new row violates row-level security policy for table "zz_opus_rls"
  ROLLBACK; POST-ROLLBACK objects | 0

RESIDUAL, HONESTLY: one narrow case is genuinely uncovered. `grant all on all functions in schema public to anon, authenticated` alone hands EXECUTE back, and no self-check reads any function ACL. Proved live: fn acl BEFORE `postgres=X/postgres` -> AFTER `postgres=X/postgres anon=X/postgres authenticated=X/postgres`, with all nine self-checks unaffected. That is a real defense-in-depth gap worth adding a check for, but it is not the claimed exploit: no documented route in this repo grants functions without also granting tables, and the tables half trips the TRUNCATE canary.

Confidence is "likely" not "certain" only because the local `postgres` database was empty when I ran (0 public tables — another agent mid-reset), so I proved the mechanisms on synthetic objects rather than on calculation_results itself. The mechanisms tested (ALL includes TRUNCATE; RLS-with-no-INSERT-policy denies a granted role) are role- and schema-independent PostgreSQL semantics, so the conclusion does not depend on that.

I tried hard to refute this and could only correct it, not kill it.

STRUCTURAL CLAIM — CONFIRMED by direct read of scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs. `const SELF_CHECKS = [` is at line 252 and holds exactly nine checks (grep of `name:` from line 252 on): auth_schema_and_helpers_present (254), auth_user_foreign_keys_present (277), policy_functions_resolve (301), tables_without_rls (314), rls_without_policies (327), tables_without_insert_policy (344), api_roles_hold_their_grants (383), truncate_granted_to_api_roles (402), security_definer_without_search_path (414). None queries INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on calculation_results or EXECUTE on record_calculation_result. `truncate_granted_to_api_roles` filters `privilege_type = 'TRUNCATE'` only; `api_roles_hold_their_grants` fires only when a role holds ZERO grants in public — it cannot fire when grants are too WIDE. `effective_grants` (123) and `function_grants` (169) are in CHECKS, skipped in --check mode (`const selfOnly = args[0] === "--check"` at 510; the CHECKS loop is inside `if (!selfOnly)`). "RESULT: POSTURE MATCHES" / exit 0 is line 599 (finding said 598, trivially off).

WHERE I CORRECT THE FINDING. Its exploit step 4 ("permits an ordinary authenticated member to INSERT a fabricated embedded_emissions_tco2e directly into calculation_results") is FALSE. 20260903190000 does two things: `drop policy if exists calculation_results_insert_own_org_as_self` (line 144) AND `revoke insert, update, delete ... from anon, authenticated`. After it, the only policy left on the table is calculation_results_select_own_org (grep of create/drop policy across supabase/migrations shows exactly this). RLS with no INSERT policy denies the write regardless of grants. Proved live in a real BEGIN...ROLLBACK against 127.0.0.1:54322, replicating the post-migration shape (RLS on, SELECT-only policy, writes revoked), then restoring the blanket table grant:
  A: table grants now | 6
  set local role authenticated; insert ... -> ERROR: new row violates row-level security policy for table "zz_probe_calcres"
  ROLLBACK; POST-ROLLBACK table exists? | f

WHERE THE FINDING SURVIVES — the RPC path, which is the half that actually matters. record_calculation_result is SECURITY DEFINER, so it bypasses RLS, and it accepts p_embedded_emissions_tco2e unchecked (it validates determination, quantity, membership, capability — never the number; the migration header says so explicitly: "the member would simply pass the forged number to the function instead of to the table"). Restoring the grant with the blanket form that both the hosted bootstrap and pre-72701dd seed.sql use reopens it. Proved live, same transaction discipline:
  grant all on all functions in schema public to anon, authenticated, service_role;
  B: authenticated has EXECUTE? | t
  set local role authenticated; select public.zz_record(...,'0.001') -> OK
  B: forged row landed | n=1 | forged=0.001
and every self-check's own SQL returned zero offending rows on that same state: tables_without_rls 0, rls_without_policies 0, security_definer_without_search_path 0 (the function carries `set search_path = public`). ROLLBACK; POST-ROLLBACK exists | f.

ALREADY-MITIGATED LENS — I searched and found three mitigations, none of which closes this:
1. tests/integration/calculation-reproduction.test.ts:886 case "(4) grants no INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE ... at all" asserts the member's RPC call returns "permission denied" (lines 915-935). Real coverage — but it runs in `pnpm test` against the dev/CI database, not against a restored target; the runbook never prescribes it as a restore acceptance step (grep of BACKUP_RESTORE.md for pnpm test finds only line 209 "never restore over the database pnpm test uses" and line 713 about the drill's own writes).
2. supabase/seed.sql (post-72701dd) re-asserts both revokes after the blanket grants — that fixes the seed path only, not a dump/PITR/bootstrap path. Note its own comment overstates the same thing the finding does: it claims "the blanket table grant handed all three back, and the forgery ... was reachable again". The table grant alone does not, per probe A; the FUNCTION grant clause is what makes that sentence true.
3. Two-DSN mode does cover it: function_grants (169) and effective_grants (123) are both `critical: true` and would diff the ACL. The finding concedes this itself.

NOTE ON ENVIRONMENT: the local Postgres at 54322 currently holds ZERO tables in public and no supabase_migrations schema (`select count(*) from information_schema.tables where table_schema='public'` -> 0), so no full-schema reproduction was possible; I reproduced the exact Postgres semantics on a synthetic mirror of the post-migration shape instead, and left the database as I found it (both probes rolled back, verified by to_regclass returning null after).

SEVERITY: HIGH overstates it. This is a blind spot in a verification tool, not a live hole in the release candidate — the RC's own database is correct, and the exploit needs an independent posture regression to happen first. The two-DSN form (the acceptance form the runbook prescribes at BACKUP_RESTORE.md:525 for "after restoring, compare the restored target against the source") does catch it, and --check's documented primary role at line 633 is a pre-restore prerequisite probe. What genuinely remains is that --check prints the identical "RESULT: POSTURE MATCHES" verdict on a database where the P14.1 function-grant boundary has been reverted, and the same-day seed.sql incident proves that reversion is an ordinary event rather than a hypothetical. MEDIUM.

title: Four of the six rejection-reason mappings in the release-blocker fix's application layer have no test
evidence:
src/application/calculations/calculate-line.ts:307-324 maps the writer's rejection onto the user-facing reason through a five-branch ladder:
  SHIPMENT_NOT_EDITABLE -> SHIPMENT_NOT_EDITABLE
  LINE_NOT_FOUND        -> LINE_NOT_FOUND
  ACTOR_NOT_A_MEMBER    -> ACTOR_NO_LONGER_A_MEMBER
  CAPABILITY_NOT_HELD   -> CAPABILITY_NOT_HELD
  (DETERMINATION_MISMATCH / QUANTITY_MISMATCH / LINE_HAS_NO_QUANTITY fall through) -> CALCULATION_INPUTS_CHANGED
plus an earlier guard at line 269-281 returning CALCULATION_INPUTS_CHANGED when line.emission_determination is null.

Every mockWriter outcome used in src/application/calculations/calculate-line.test.ts (grep of `mockWriter(` and the outcome literals at lines 248, 288, 356, 388, 422, 446-449, 471-475, 515, 590, 647, 683, 701): exactly two non-default outcomes are ever constructed — `{ status: "FAILED", message: "db error" }` at line 449 and `{ status: "REJECTED", reason: "SHIPMENT_NOT_EDITABLE" }` at line 475. LINE_NOT_FOUND at lines 394/430 is the line-fetch path, not a writer rejection.

A repository-wide grep confirms CALCULATION_INPUTS_CHANGED and ACTOR_NO_LONGER_A_MEMBER appear only in calculate-line.ts and app/(importer)/shipments/[id]/actions.ts:1113,1115 — never in any test file.
exploit: No exploit; this is missing coverage on the newest, least-exercised code in the release blocker's fix. The fall-through branch is the security-relevant one: DETERMINATION_MISMATCH and QUANTITY_MISMATCH are the two bindings the old RLS policy never had, and the only ones that fire when a member's determination or quantity does not match the line. A refactor that reordered or dropped a branch — mapping ACTOR_NOT_A_MEMBER to CALCULATION_INPUTS_CHANGED, say — would tell the user to 'reload the line and calculate it again' when their membership has actually been revoked, and no test would notice.
impact: Wrong or misleading refusal messages on the calculation path, and no regression net under the newest code in the blocker fix. Confined to UI messaging: the database-side refusals themselves are well covered by calculation-reproduction.test.ts cases (5) and (6), which assert DETERMINATION_MISMATCH, QUANTITY_MISMATCH, ACTOR_NOT_A_MEMBER and LINE_NOT_FOUND by name against the real RPC.
freshEnvironment: Yes. Established by reading the committed test file's mockWriter call sites and by grepping the two new reason strings across the whole repository; no database involved.

verdicts.reasoning:
I re-ran the finding's own evidence rather than trusting it, and its FACTS are accurate — but under the reachability lens the claimed impact does not exist, and the branch count is wrong.

WHAT I CONFIRMED (the finding is not fabricated):
- src/application/calculations/calculate-line.ts:307-324 is exactly the five-branch ternary ladder described (read directly).
- grep of src/application/calculations/calculate-line.test.ts for `mockWriter(` and every reason literal returns non-default writer outcomes at ONLY two sites: line 449 `status: "FAILED"` and lines 474-475 `status: "REJECTED", reason: "SHIPMENT_NOT_EDITABLE"`. All other call sites (288, 356, 388, 422, 515, 590, 647, 683, 701) use the default `{status:"OK", calculation_id:"calc-1"}` defined at test:252-255.
- The two LINE_NOT_FOUND assertions (test:394, test:430) are indeed the line-fetch path — I read test:375-435: both pass `mockWriter()` (default OK) and drive `mockSupabase({lineFetchResult:{data:null}})` / an `org_id:"org-2"` row. Not the writer branch.
- The CAPABILITY_NOT_HELD test (test:668-691) is the pre-database gate: its fake supabase `from` throws "calculateLine must not read the database before the capability check runs". Not the writer branch.
- Repo-wide grep (excluding node_modules) for CALCULATION_INPUTS_CHANGED / ACTOR_NO_LONGER_A_MEMBER returns only calculate-line.ts:67,72,279,317,324 and app/(importer)/shipments/[id]/actions.ts:1113,1115. Zero test files.

WHY IT IS REFUTED AS A MEDIUM DEFECT:

1. No reachable wrong behavior exists. I read the ladder line by line; every mapping is correct as written. The claimed impact is explicitly counterfactual — "a refactor that reordered or dropped a branch". That refactor has not happened. Under a reachability lens the actor is a hypothetical future editor, not a real one, and the finding itself states "No exploit."

2. One of the six paths is provably unreachable, so counting it as missing coverage is wrong. The guard at calculate-line.ts:269-281 sits AFTER `if (calculation.status !== "COMPUTED") return {status:"OK", calculation}` (calculate-line.ts:233-238). src/domain/calculations/calculate-line-emissions.ts:391-395 begins `if (!line.emission_determination) { return noValueResult("INPUT_UNRESOLVED"); }` — a null determination can never yield COMPUTED, so that branch cannot be entered through the public entry point without lying to the type system. The code's own comment says "Unreachable through the engine" and it is correct.

3. The four remaining writer-rejection branches are reachable only through a millisecond-wide TOCTOU window. calculate-line.ts:182-189 SELECTs the line, then :283-299 passes back the same `line.emission_determination` and `quantityInput(line)` it just read to an RPC that re-reads and compares. DETERMINATION_MISMATCH / QUANTITY_MISMATCH / LINE_HAS_NO_QUANTITY require the line to be edited between those two reads; ACTOR_NOT_A_MEMBER and writer-side CAPABILITY_NOT_HELD require membership/capability revocation inside the same window (the org context was already resolved from a live member row upstream in actions.ts).

4. The consequence is confined to one sentence of UI copy, and no security boundary rides on it. The refusal itself is enforced in the database and IS covered live: tests/integration/calculation-reproduction.test.ts asserts LINE_NOT_FOUND (:987), DETERMINATION_MISMATCH (:1021), QUANTITY_MISMATCH (:1044), ACTOR_NOT_A_MEMBER (:1067) by name against the real `record_calculation_result` RPC. The infrastructure writer (src/infrastructure/calculations/get-calculation-result-writer.ts) also refuses to guess: an unknown `result_status` becomes FAILED, never "the nearest known reason". A mis-mapped string would show wrong copy; it could not admit a forged emissions figure.

5. No fresh-environment / ordering hazard is involved — this is a static reading of a committed test file, so the seed-regrant failure class this review is hunting does not apply.

Net: a real but cosmetic test-hygiene gap on correct, mostly race-only-reachable code whose security-relevant half is covered by live-database integration tests. Not MEDIUM; INFO at most.
