title: No test in the repository asserts a database privilege, and the one test titled as if it does asserts something else
evidence:
tests/integration/calculation-reproduction.test.ts:~885 is titled '(4) grants no INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE on calculation_results to anon or authenticated at all', and its comment says 'The property behind tests 1-3, asserted directly rather than inferred from three refusals: no privilege, so no policy can accidentally re-open the surface later.' The body makes no privilege assertion: it calls record_calculation_result as serviceClient (expects result_status OK) and as ownerClient (expects a 'permission denied' error). No anon client is constructed anywhere in the file — LOCAL_ANON_KEY appears once, at line 254, to build the signed-in member's client.

`grep -rn "has_table_privilege|information_schema|role_table_grants|has_function_privilege" --include="*.test.ts" --include="*.spec.ts"` over the whole repository returns zero matches across all 137 test files.
exploit: NONE (structural). The consequence is that every proof of the P14.1 write boundary in the suite is behavioural — it requires a live PostgREST, a live Postgres, a seeded regulatory dataset and a signed-in member. Those preconditions hold only in the build-and-test CI job and on a fully provisioned developer host. There is no cheap, environment-independent assertion of the grant posture that a restore drill, a staging check or the fast-gates job could run — which is what leaves finding #1 with nothing standing behind it.
impact: The suite cannot distinguish 'the privilege is revoked' from 'some other wall happened to refuse this particular request', and it says nothing at all about anon. The title of case (4) overstates what it measures, which matters because that case is cited in supabase/seed.sql's own header as the test that covers the seed/migration coupling.
freshEnvironment: Yes. Verified by a repository-wide grep of all test files for any privilege-introspection call; the result is zero regardless of database state.

verdicts.reasoning:
Reproduced the grep: no test file calls has_table_privilege/information_schema/role_table_grants/has_function_privilege. That narrow fact holds. The conclusions drawn from it do not.

(a) The suite DOES assert database privileges, behaviourally and discriminatingly. tests/integration/calculation-reproduction.test.ts cases (1)(2)(3) each assert expect(error?.message).toContain("permission denied") on a member INSERT into calculation_results. Postgres emits "permission denied for table calculation_results" (missing grant) versus "new row violates row-level security policy for table ..." (RLS). The assertion selects the grant refusal, so the claim "the suite cannot distinguish the privilege is revoked from some other wall happened to refuse" is wrong. Case (4)'s body asserts rpcError?.message.toLowerCase() contains "permission denied" on the member's record_calculation_result call, which is a privilege assertion of the EXECUTE grant that supabase/migrations/20260903190000_p141_calculation_results_trusted_write_only.sql lines 353-357 give to service_role alone.

(b) These behavioural assertions demonstrably caught the exact fresh-environment failure class. supabase/seed.sql lines 73-75 record that this test case "failed in CI exactly as it should" on the first release-candidate run, which is how the blanket-grant-after-narrow-revoke defect was discovered. .github/workflows/ci.yml line 315 re-runs supabase/seed.sql explicitly, and the integration tests run after it, on a freshly built database.

(c) The claim "There is no cheap, environment-independent assertion of the grant posture that a restore drill, a staging check or the fast-gates job could run" is false. scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs does exactly that: effective_grants (line 123, information_schema.role_table_grants, critical:true), function_grants (line 169, p.proacl, critical:true), api_roles_hold_their_grants (line 383) and truncate_granted_to_api_roles (line 402) as single-database --check self-checks. The finding's grep was restricted to *.test.ts/*.spec.ts and therefore missed the tool purpose-built for the restore drill it says has nothing.

(d) Reachability of the only true residue: case (4)'s title names table INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE for "anon or authenticated" while its body tests the function EXECUTE grant; LOCAL_ANON_KEY at line 254 is indeed only used to build the signed-in member's client. That is a title imprecision. It leaves no control unproven: authenticated table DML is covered by cases (1)-(3), the RPC by (4), and an anon INSERT is unreachable irrespective of grants because calculation_results has RLS enabled and carries no INSERT policy for any role (compare-database-posture.mjs:344-371 allowlists it for that reason). No real actor path is untested.

Live re-verification was not possible: the local Postgres at 127.0.0.1:54322 is currently empty. `select count(*) from pg_tables where schemaname='public'` returned 0; `select to_regclass('public.calculation_results')` returned empty; `select ... from supabase_migrations.schema_migrations` returned ERROR: relation "supabase_migrations.schema_migrations" does not exist. Grant queries against calculation_results and pg_proc returned zero rows for the same reason, not because the grants are absent by design. The finding is database-independent, so the static evidence above is sufficient to resolve it.

Net: the headline is not sustainable, the stated impact is contradicted by an existing tool, and the surviving fact is a misleading test title with no unenforced control behind it.

That is an EXECUTE-reachability assertion on one function, not a table-privilege assertion, and it never touches INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on the table.

2. No anon client. `grep -n "LOCAL_ANON_KEY" tests/integration/calculation-reproduction.test.ts` returns lines 72-73 (constant), 86 (`headers: { apikey: LOCAL_ANON_KEY }` inside `isLocalSupabaseReachable`, a reachability fetch), and 254 (inside `signIn()`, which then calls `signInWithPassword` — i.e. the signed-in member's client). No unauthenticated client is ever exercised against `calculation_results`. The word "anon" in the title is unmeasured.

3. Zero privilege introspection in tests. Repo-wide (not just *.test.ts): `grep -rn "has_table_privilege|has_function_privilege|information_schema.role_table_grants|table_privileges|relacl|proacl|aclexplode|defacl" --include=*.ts --include=*.js --include=*.sql --include=*.py --include=*.sh --include=*.mjs --include=*.yml .` returns exactly 8 hits, ALL outside the test tree: `scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs:130,175,388,395,406` and comment lines in two migrations (`20260829590000_...:23,42`, `20260903170000_...:15`). No test file asserts any database privilege.

4. The mis-citation is load-bearing. `supabase/seed.sql:73-76` states: "See tests/integration/calculation-reproduction.test.ts ... case (4), which asserts no write grant and an unreachable RPC". Case (4) asserts only the second half. So the seed's own justification for its blanket-grant/re-revoke design cites a coverage claim that does not exist.

REFUTED — the finding's IMPACT paragraph is materially overstated on two points:

(a) "There is no cheap, environment-independent assertion of the grant posture that a restore drill, a staging check or the fast-gates job could run" is FALSE. `scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs --check <dsn>` is exactly that: single-database, `psql`-only, deliberately no npm dependency (:35-37). Its SELF_CHECKS (:252-430) include `api_roles_hold_their_grants` (:383-401, reads `information_schema.role_table_grants`) and `truncate_granted_to_api_roles` (:402-415), and its two-DB CHECKS include `effective_grants` (:122-135), `schema_usage_grants` (:136-152) and `function_grants` (:169-184). It is wired into `docs/runbooks/DEPLOYMENT.md:571-579` as rebuild step 6 and `docs/runbooks/BACKUP_RESTORE.md:520-530,633`. What is genuinely missing is narrower than claimed: no self-check covers INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on `calculation_results` (`grep -n calculation_results` in that script hits only :366,:371, the exclusion list in `tables_without_insert_policy`).

(b) "The suite cannot distinguish 'the privilege is revoked' from 'some other wall'" is weak for `authenticated`. Cases (1)-(3) at :~800-882 assert the exact substring `"permission denied"` on a member INSERT. Since `calculation_results` carries no INSERT policy, a re-granted surface would produce "new row violates row-level security policy", not "permission denied" — so those three cases would fail on the seed/migration coupling regression. The gap is real for `anon` only, and it is a coverage gap rather than a blindness.

I could not run the live confirmation: the local cluster's public schema is currently empty — `PGPASSWORD=postgres psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 54322 -U postgres -d postgres -tAc "select count(*) from information_schema.tables where table_schema='public';"` returns `0`, and `select to_regclass('public.calculation_results')` returns NULL. That does not affect this finding, which is fully decidable from the repository, and it is itself consistent with the finding's point that every proof of this boundary needs a fully provisioned host.

Net: the finding stands as written on its evidence (test title, test comment, and a seed.sql citation all assert coverage the body does not provide; no test in the repo introspects a privilege). Its severity is correctly LOW — no exploit, no behavioural gap for `authenticated`, and a grant checker does exist outside the test suite.

title: A unit test cites a database-side proof in a test file that does not exist
evidence:
src/application/calculations/calculate-line.test.ts:246 — 'The one field that left them is `shipment_id`, because the RPC now DERIVES it from the line rather than accepting it from the caller -- a stronger guarantee than asserting the caller passed the right one, and one proved on the database side in tests/integration/calculation-result-write-boundary.test.ts.'

`ls tests/integration/` lists seventeen files; calculation-result-write-boundary.test.ts is not among them. `grep -rn "calculation-result-write-boundary"` across the repository returns exactly one hit: that comment itself.

The proof does exist, under a different name: the describe block 'P14.1 -- the calculation-result write boundary' inside tests/integration/calculation-reproduction.test.ts, whose case (7) asserts the derived shipment_id.
exploit: NONE (structural). A reviewer verifying the claim by opening the named file finds nothing and must either guess or conclude the coverage is absent.
impact: Traceability only. The assertion the comment describes is genuinely present elsewhere, so no behaviour is unproved — but in a codebase whose whole review discipline is 'check the claim, not the comment', a citation to a file that was never created is the kind of thing that turns into a withdrawn claim two audits later.
freshEnvironment: Yes. Established by directory listing and a repository-wide grep; nothing environment-dependent.

verdicts.reasoning:
Re-ran every element of the finding's evidence from scratch; all of it holds, and nothing about it is environment-dependent.

1. The citation exists exactly where claimed. `sed -n '243,247p' src/application/calculations/calculate-line.test.ts` puts the text on line 246:
   ` * and one proved on the database side in`
   ` * tests/integration/calculation-result-write-boundary.test.ts.`

2. The cited file does not exist. `ls tests/integration/` returns seventeen entries: audit-events-occurred-at-hardening, auth-email-links, calculation-reproduction, declarations-isolation, emission-data-write-hardening, importer-entered-provenance, module-load, organizations-isolation, regulatory-authenticated-read, regulatory-repository, regulatory-resolution, shared-data-consumption-audit, shared-data-status-visibility, sharing-counterparty-names, sharing-grants-isolation, shipment-line-determination-hardening, shipments-isolation. `calculation-result-write-boundary.test.ts` is absent.

3. Repository-wide grep confirms the name appears nowhere but in the comment itself:
   `grep -rn "calculation-result-write-boundary" . --exclude-dir=node_modules --exclude-dir=.git`
   -> `./src/application/calculations/calculate-line.test.ts:246: * tests/integration/calculation-result-write-boundary.test.ts.`
   Exactly one hit, and it is the dangling citation. There is no file, no import, no config entry, no rename mapping.

4. The described proof genuinely exists under a different name, as the finding says. In D:/projects/snowkap-cbam/tests/integration/calculation-reproduction.test.ts:
   - line 724: `describe("P14.1 -- the calculation-result write boundary", ...)`
   - line 1073: `it("(7) accepts a legitimate calculation result, and derives shipment_id and calculated_at itself", ...)`
   - lines 1118-1120: `// Derived, not accepted: the caller never sent a shipment_id.` / `expect(stored.shipment_id).toBe(shipmentId);`
   So the substantive guarantee is proved; only the pointer is wrong.

REACHABILITY LENS. This finding is not a privilege or RLS claim, so there is no exploit path to disprove and no capability to check against the database. The "actor" is a reviewer or maintainer following a citation that the codebase's own review discipline invites them to follow, and that path is fully real: the comment is on a live line of a file in the release candidate, and following it lands on nothing. There is no mitigating indirection -- no alias, no barrel file, no vitest include pattern that would make the named path resolve. I checked for the failure class this review is hunting (a claim true only of this build/ordering) and it does not apply in either direction: the defect is established by a directory listing and a static grep, so it is equally true of a freshly built environment.

Severity: LOW, as claimed. No behaviour is unproved and no regulatory or security control is affected -- the write-boundary assertion is present and passing under a different filename. The cost is traceability: a citation to a file that was never created, in a codebase whose stated method is "check the claim, not the comment". The fix is a one-line correction of the path to tests/integration/calculation-reproduction.test.ts (optionally naming the describe block and case (7)).

Every claim in the finding reproduces exactly.

1. The quoted comment is verbatim. `sed -n '225,265p' src/application/calculations/calculate-line.test.ts` shows lines 243-246: "...a stronger guarantee than asserting the caller passed the right one, and one proved on the database side in / tests/integration/calculation-result-write-boundary.test.ts." Line 246 is the filename line, matching the cited file:line precisely.

2. The cited file does not exist. `ls tests/integration/` returns exactly seventeen entries (audit-events-occurred-at-hardening, auth-email-links, calculation-reproduction, declarations-isolation, emission-data-write-hardening, importer-entered-provenance, module-load, organizations-isolation, regulatory-authenticated-read, regulatory-repository, regulatory-resolution, shared-data-consumption-audit, shared-data-status-visibility, sharing-counterparty-names, sharing-grants-isolation, shipment-line-determination-hardening, shipments-isolation) — no calculation-result-write-boundary.test.ts.

3. Repository-wide grep for "calculation-result-write-boundary" (excluding node_modules) returns exactly one hit: `./src/application/calculations/calculate-line.test.ts:246` — the comment itself. Nothing else references it.

4. I went further than the finding did: `find . -name "*write-boundary*" -not -path "*/node_modules/*"` returns nothing, and `git log --all --diff-filter=A --name-only` filtered for "write-boundary" returns nothing — the file was never added on any branch in history, so this is not a rename whose old name lingered, it is a citation to a file that never existed.

5. The finding's exculpatory half is also correct: `grep -n` on tests/integration/calculation-reproduction.test.ts shows line 723-724 `describe(` / `"P14.1 -- the calculation-result write boundary"`, and line 1072-1073 `it(` / `"(7) accepts a legitimate calculation result, and derives shipment_id and calculated_at itself"`, with line 1118-1119 `// Derived, not accepted: the caller never sent a shipment_id.` / `expect(stored.shipment_id).toBe(`. The database-side proof the comment describes is genuinely present, just in a differently-named file.

Nothing here is environment-dependent, so no database probe applies; the local Postgres could not change the answer.

I cannot refute this. The only correction I would make is to severity and framing: this is a stale cross-reference inside a source comment, not a false claim in an audit document, and the substantive assertion is real and reachable — the describe block carries the same wording as the invented filename, so a grep on the phrase finds it immediately. Category AUDIT_HONESTY slightly overstates a comment-level traceability slip. INFO rather than LOW.

Could not refute; confirmed by independent re-verification of all three claims.

(1) Comment verified verbatim at src/application/calculations/calculate-line.test.ts:246: " * tests/integration/calculation-result-write-boundary.test.ts." closing the sentence "...and one proved on the database side in".

(2) Cited file does not exist and NEVER existed. `ls tests/integration/` returns 17 files, none matching. `grep -rn "calculation-result-write-boundary" .` (excluding node_modules) returns exactly one hit -- the comment itself, at line 246. `find . -name "*write-boundary*" -not -path "*/node_modules/*"` returns nothing. Decisively: `git rev-list --all --objects | grep -c "calculation-result-write-boundary"` returns 0, and `git log --diff-filter=R --name-status -- tests/integration/` shows no renames. So this is not a stale pointer to a renamed file -- the file was never created in any commit on any branch.

(3) The proof genuinely exists elsewhere as the finding states: tests/integration/calculation-reproduction.test.ts:724 opens describe("P14.1 -- the calculation-result write boundary", ...); case (7) at line 1073 is "(7) accepts a legitimate calculation result, and derives shipment_id and calculated_at itself", and lines 1118-1121 read: "// Derived, not accepted: the caller never sent a shipment_id." followed by expect(stored.shipment_id).toBe(shipmentId); -- exactly the assertion the comment describes.

ALREADY-MITIGATED LENS -- searched, no mitigation found. No link/reference checker exists in the toolchain: package.json scripts are only dev, build, postbuild, start, test, test:watch, test:e2e, typecheck, regulatory:verify. Nothing validates file paths inside comments, so no gate catches this. I also checked whether the audit document repeats the error -- it does not: docs/plans/P14_FINAL_RELEASE_AUDIT.md:1233-1235 correctly attributes the cases to "tests/integration/calculation-reproduction.test.ts gains **\"P14.1 - the calculation-result write boundary\"**, ten cases against real Postgres". The error is isolated to the single code comment. Partial mitigation for the record: grepping the prose phrase "write boundary" (not the hyphenated filename) does land on calculation-reproduction.test.ts:724, so recovery is possible but requires guessing the right search term.

Severity: LOW retained, not downgraded to INFO. No behaviour is unproved, but the comment's entire function is to justify a deliberately weakened assertion set (removal of shipment_id from the payload checks) by pointing at compensating coverage, and it points at nothing. Purely structural; nothing environment-dependent, so no database probe was applicable.

title: seed.sql's blanket function grant leaves anon holding EXECUTE on seven SECURITY DEFINER RPCs the migrations granted only to authenticated
evidence:
supabase/seed.sql: `grant all on all functions in schema public to anon, authenticated, service_role;` runs after every migration. The migrations grant these to `authenticated` only (e.g. 20260828080000:108, 20260828130000:303, 20260829330000:1031, 20260829310000:332, 20260831100000:96) and revoke from the PUBLIC pseudo-role, which the blanket grant does not restore — but it does add anon.

Measured on the local database:
  select p.proname, has_function_privilege('anon', p.oid, 'execute') from pg_proc p where p.pronamespace='public'::regnamespace and p.prokind='f';
  accept_organization_invitation|t
  accept_sharing_grant_invitation|t
  create_organization_with_owner|t
  list_org_members|t
  record_calculation_result|f
  record_declaration_filed|t
  record_shared_data_consumption|t
  sharing_counterparty_org_names|t

No test asserts anything about anon's execute privileges (see the zero-hit privilege grep in the finding above).
exploit: Probed live, read-only, and it does not currently go anywhere. `begin; set local role anon; set local request.jwt.claims = '{"role":"anon"}'; select * from public.create_organization_with_owner('Probe Org','IMPORTER','{IMPORTER_DECLARANT}'); rollback;` returns ERROR: create_organization_with_owner requires an authenticated caller. The same shape against public.sharing_counterparty_org_names() returns 0 rows. Each function defends itself on auth.uid() rather than on the grant.
impact: None today — reported because the defence rests entirely on each function's own internal check, with no privilege-level backstop and no test. record_calculation_result is the one function seed.sql explicitly re-revokes, which shows the author knew the blanket grant reaches functions; the other seven were left to defend themselves. A future RPC added to schema public inherits EXECUTE for anon automatically, and nothing in the suite or in compare-database-posture.mjs's self-checks would flag it.
freshEnvironment: Yes, and more so: this is the state a fresh `supabase db reset` / `supabase start` produces by construction, because seed.sql's blanket grant is the last statement to run. Measured on this database, which is in exactly that state for functions (the migrations post-date the last seed only for the three objects seed.sql now re-revokes).

verdicts.reasoning:
I could not refute it. The mechanism reproduces exactly; the reachability lens confirms zero exploitability, which is what the finding itself claims, so INFO stands.

WHAT I COULD NOT RE-RUN. The finding's own measurement is not reproducible against the local DB in its current state — the local Postgres at 127.0.0.1:54322 has NO project migrations applied at all:
  select nspname, count(*) from pg_proc p join pg_namespace n on n.oid=p.pronamespace group by 1;
  -> pg_catalog|3319, extensions|55, realtime|15, information_schema|11, vault|5, auth|4, pgbouncer|1, graphql_public|1  (no `public`, no `app` rows)
  select count(*) from supabase_migrations.schema_migrations;
  -> ERROR: relation "supabase_migrations.schema_migrations" does not exist
So the DB was reset/wiped since the finding was written. I re-derived the claim from source plus a controlled reproduction instead.

MECHANISM REPRODUCED (throwaway db `refute_probe`, created and dropped in the local cluster). Replicated the exact migration pattern used at supabase/migrations/20260828080000_organization_onboarding_rpc.sql:107-108:
  create function public.probe_rpc() ... security definer;
  revoke all on function public.probe_rpc() from public;
  grant execute on function public.probe_rpc() to authenticated;
  -> anon=f | auth=t | acl: postgres=X/postgres | authenticated=X/postgres
Then supabase/seed.sql:23 verbatim:
  grant all on all functions in schema public to anon, authenticated, service_role;
  -> anon=t | acl: postgres=X/postgres | authenticated=X/postgres | anon=X/postgres | service_role=X/postgres
The revoke targets the PUBLIC pseudo-role; the blanket grant adds anon explicitly. Confirmed.

ORDERING CONFIRMED. supabase/config.toml:66-68 `[db.seed] enabled = true` — "seeds the database after migrations during a db reset". supabase/seed.sql:1-4 states the CLI runs it "as the final step of `supabase db reset`/`start`". So the fresh-environment claim is correct by construction. Worse than the finding says: seed.sql:31-32 also runs `alter default privileges in schema public grant all on functions to anon, authenticated, service_role;`, so any future public RPC inherits anon EXECUTE at CREATE time — the finding's forward-looking claim is backed by an actual statement, not just inference.

INVENTORY MATCHES. `grep create function public.` across supabase/migrations/ yields exactly the 8 functions the finding lists: accept_organization_invitation, accept_sharing_grant_invitation, create_organization_with_owner, list_org_members, record_calculation_result, record_declaration_filed, record_shared_data_consumption, sharing_counterparty_org_names. Only record_calculation_result is re-revoked (supabase/seed.sql:92-97).

REACHABILITY (the lens I was told to apply). The route exists and the capability is held: anon is PostgREST's unauthenticated role and /rest/v1/rpc/<fn> is a real, internet-reachable path with the public anon key. So this is NOT refuted on "no route / no capability". It is refuted only on impact, and the finding already concedes that. I read all seven bodies myself:
  - create_organization_with_owner (20260828080000:66-68), accept_organization_invitation (20260828130000:188-190), accept_sharing_grant_invitation (20260829390000:173-175), record_shared_data_consumption (20260829310000:128-130), record_declaration_filed (20260829330000:628-630): each opens with `if auth.uid() is null then raise exception '... requires an authenticated caller.'`
  - list_org_members (20260829360000:283-289): `if not exists (select 1 from app.user_org_ids() as caller_org_id where caller_org_id = p_org_id) then raise exception 'Not a member of this organization.'` — app.user_org_ids() filters `user_id = auth.uid()`, null for anon, so 0 rows, so it raises.
  - sharing_counterparty_org_names (20260902150000:126-175): plain SQL, no explicit guard, but both branches gate on `in (select app.user_org_ids())`, empty for anon, so it returns 0 rows and discloses nothing.
No leak on any of the seven.

SCOPE CONSTRAINT THE FINDING UNDERSTATES (argues for keeping it at INFO, not raising it). supabase/seed.sql:1-4 says it is "never applied to any hosted Supabase project". Production is provisioned by `supabase db push`, which does not run seed.sql. So this posture drift exists only in local dev and CI databases, never in the hosted environment. The finding's "fresh environment" framing is right but the blast radius is developer machines only.

TEST-GAP CLAIM CONFIRMED. `grep -rn "has_function_privilege|has_table_privilege|proacl|relacl|routine_privileges" tests/ scripts/` returns exactly one hit, scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs:175 — a local-vs-hosted comparison report, not an assertion, and not a gate. tests/integration/calculation-reproduction.test.ts:724 ("P14.1 -- the calculation-result write boundary") exercises only record_calculation_result — the one function seed re-revokes. Nothing asserts anything about anon's EXECUTE on the other seven.

VERDICT: factually accurate, mechanism independently reproduced, correctly self-rated. It is a defense-in-depth / missing-backstop observation with no exploitable consequence and a local-only blast radius. INFO is right; it should not be raised, and I have no basis to strike it.

Scratch work: throwaway database `refute_probe` created and dropped (`DROP DATABASE` confirmed; remaining `refute_probe_tmp` is another agent's and was left untouched). No repository file was read-modified, created or deleted; no writes to production.

I tried to refute this on the correctness lens and could not. Every cited fact is accurate.

THE SEED STATEMENT EXISTS AS QUOTED. `supabase/seed.sql:23`: `grant all on all functions in schema public to anon, authenticated, service_role;` (also `:32` `alter default privileges ... grant all on functions to anon, authenticated, service_role;`). Its own re-revoke block at `:79-101` revokes `record_calculation_result` from `public, anon, authenticated` and re-grants to `service_role` only — which is why that one function measures `f` for anon and the other seven measure `t`.    - `20260828130000_organization_invitations.sql:302-303` (accept_organization_invitation)
   - `20260829310000_p7d3_shared_data_consumption_audit.sql:331-332` (record_shared_data_consumption)

The one place `proacl` appears (`:175`, the `function_grants` capture) is a two-environment drift comparison, not an absolute assertion, so it flags nothing when both sides are built identically. DEPLOYMENT.md:577-578 names only `truncate_granted_to_api_roles` and `tables_without_insert_policy` as the verification step, consistent with the finding.

The defence is genuinely internal to each function, exactly as the finding states, with no privilege-level backstop behind it.

Nothing in the finding is overstated; if anything the runbook evidence in (5) makes it slightly stronger than written. Confirmed at INFO.

CONFIRMED. I could not refute it on any of the mitigation lenses.

`revoke ... from public` (the PUBLIC pseudo-role) does not remove an explicit `anon` grant.

- Test coverage: `grep -rn "has_function_privilege|proacl|role_routine_grants|routine_privileges" tests/ scripts/ docs/` returns ZERO hits outside scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs. tests/integration/calculation-reproduction.test.ts:886 case (4) asserts only record_calculation_result's unreachability ("permission denied") — it says nothing about anon or the other seven.

title: Third vacuous pass in `auth_user_foreign_keys_present`: it fires only at exactly zero while its own message says 'expected 10'
evidence:
scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs:286-297. The message is `'NO product foreign key references auth.users -- expected 10'` but the predicate is `where ( select count(*) ... ) = 0`. Nine of ten missing is a pass.

Proven on throwaway probe2 (a clean restore where the check first reported [OK] with all 10 present). I dropped nine of the ten constraints, then:

  select count(*) from pg_constraint con join pg_class c on c.oid=con.confrelid
   join pg_namespace cn on cn.oid=c.relnamespace join pg_class r on r.oid=con.conrelid
   join pg_namespace rn on rn.oid=r.relnamespace
   where con.contype='f' and cn.nspname='auth' and c.relname='users'
     and rn.nspname in ('public','app');
  -> 1

  node scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs --check <probe2>
  -> [OK] auth_user_foreign_keys_present
  -> RESULT: POSTURE MATCHES

The comment above that predicate (lines 280-285) says an earlier version 'passed on a project holding none of this application's schema at all. That is the same vacuous-pass this file exists to prevent.' The rewrite narrowed the scope and left the exact-zero threshold in place.
exploit: NONE -- structural. It is the detector that fails, not a reachable path. The realistic trigger is BACKUP_RESTORE.md's own D.2 case: `auth.users` restored incompletely from the provider backup, so some referenced user ids are absent and only some FKs can be created. The audit itself records nine of ten failing to create for exactly that reason.
impact: An operator running the documented pre-cutover gate on a database that lost nine of ten `auth.users` referential-integrity rules is told the restore is sound. Those FKs are what stop a membership, an audit event or a calculation result naming a user that does not exist; without them, deleting a user leaves dangling attribution on an append-only compliance record and the application's assumption that `calculated_by_user_id` resolves is no longer enforced anywhere.
freshEnvironment: Yes -- it is a property of the script's SQL, independent of any database. I demonstrated it on a throwaway restore (probe2) rather than on the working database, and dropped that database afterwards.

verdicts.reasoning:
CONFIRMED by independent re-check; I could not refute it.

CODE: scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs:277-299. Check `auth_user_foreign_keys_present` (SELF_CHECKS, treated as CRITICAL at lines 573-591 where any SELF_CHECK failure increments criticalFailures). Message: `select 'NO product foreign key references auth.users -- expected 10'`; predicate: `where ( select count(*) ... ) = 0`. Message and predicate disagree exactly as the finding states. The comment at 280-285 narrowed scope to rn.nspname in ('public','app') but left the exact-zero threshold.

LIVE RE-RUN (my own throwaway db probe_fk_refute_op5, created then dropped; the finding's probe2 no longer existed):
  created schema auth + auth.users, plus public.t1..t10 each `references auth.users(id)`.
  count query -> 10
  node scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs --check "postgresql://postgres:postgres@127.0.0.1:54322/probe_fk_refute_op5"
    -> [OK] auth_user_foreign_keys_present
  then dropped 9 of the 10 constraints; count query -> 1
  same command again
    -> [OK] auth_user_foreign_keys_present
Nine of ten missing is a pass. Predicate confirmed empirically, not just by reading.

REACHABILITY LENS (this strengthens the finding):
1. `--check <dsn>` is a documented operator gate, not a hypothetical call: docs/runbooks/DEPLOYMENT.md:571-578 (post-migration/seed "Verify the security posture survived, rather than assuming it") and docs/runbooks/BACKUP_RESTORE.md:529-530 and 633-636.
2. The 1-of-10 state is documented measured fact in this repo, not speculation: docs/runbooks/BACKUP_RESTORE.md:576-590 — "Nine of the ten foreign keys still could not be created", with the memberships_user_id_fkey ALTER TABLE error quoted, because auth.users was empty. One constraint did create. Running --check against that very drill database prints [OK].
3. Single-DSN mode is exactly the disaster mode BACKUP_RESTORE.md:529 describes ("against a restored target on its own, before a source is available") — when no source exists to compare against, this is the only gate.
4. No other SELF_CHECK covers foreign keys; I read all eight (lines 252-430).

NOTE (incidental, not part of this finding): the live local `postgres` database currently holds 0 public tables and 0 product FKs to auth.users — another agent's activity, not mine. I did not modify it. Repo untouched (git status --porcelain empty); throwaway database dropped.

Severity: HIGH stands. It is a critical-marked detector that reports a sound restore on a database the project's own drill measured as missing nine of ten referential-integrity rules, in the one mode available when the source is gone.

I tried to refute this and could not; every element of the claim checks out against the code and against a live reproduction I ran myself.

1. THE CODE SAYS WHAT THE FINDING QUOTES. scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs:277-298. Line 286 emits the literal string `'NO product foreign key references auth.users -- expected 10'`; line 297 closes the predicate with `) = 0`. So the failure row is produced only when the count is EXACTLY zero. The comment at lines 280-285 does say the earlier version "passed on a project holding none of this application's schema at all. That is the same vacuous-pass this file exists to prevent." The rewrite scoped `rn.nspname in ('public','app')` (line 296) but left the exact-zero threshold.

2. THE RUNNER TREATS ZERO ROWS AS PASS. Lines 585-586: `if (rows.length === 0) { console.log(\`[OK] ${check.name}\`); continue; }`. So 1-of-10 present yields no row, hence `[OK]`.

3. LIVE REPRODUCTION ON MY OWN THROWAWAY DB (created and dropped; I did not touch the working `postgres` db or production). Created `refute_fkthresh`, `create schema auth; create table auth.users(id uuid primary key);` then 10 public tables each with `user_id uuid references auth.users(id)`.

   Baseline — the script's own predicate SQL returned `10`, and:
     node scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs --check "postgresql://postgres:postgres@127.0.0.1:54322/refute_fkthresh"
     -> [OK] auth_user_foreign_keys_present

   Dropped 9 of the 10 constraints (t2..t10). Predicate SQL returned `1`. Re-ran:
     -> [OK] auth_user_foreign_keys_present

   Dropped the tenth. Predicate SQL returned `0`. Re-ran:
     -> [FAIL] auth_user_foreign_keys_present -- CRITICAL
        offending rows (1):
          - NO product foreign key references auth.users -- expected 10

   That is the bug exactly as described: 9-of-10 missing passes; only 10-of-10 missing fails. Cleanup: `drop database refute_fkthresh;` -> `DROP DATABASE`.

4. IT IS A DOCUMENTED GATE, AND THE VULNERABLE MODE IS THE DOCUMENTED STANDALONE ONE. docs/runbooks/BACKUP_RESTORE.md:519-531 makes this script "the acceptance test ... no longer a checklist a human reads", and explicitly documents the single-database form `--check "<dsn>"` (line 530) for use "against a restored target on its own, before a source is available" (line 529). Line 633-636 instructs running `--check` against the target before restoring. In that standalone mode there is no source database, so the `constraints` comparison in CHECKS cannot compensate — this self-check is the only thing asserting the FKs exist. (In two-database mode the constraint diff would catch it; the finding's impact is correctly scoped to the `--check` gate.)

5. FRESH-ENVIRONMENT CLAIM IS CORRECT. This is a property of the script's SQL, not of any particular database state, so it is environment-independent by construction.

TWO NOTES THAT DO NOT CHANGE THE VERDICT:
- The "expected 10" constant is itself slightly off. `grep -rin "references auth\.users" supabase/migrations/` returns 12 hits, of which one (20260829360000_p10_membership_deactivation.sql:13) is a comment, leaving 11 real `references auth.users(id)` clauses across 10 migrations. The message's hardcoded "10" is at best unverified. This strengthens rather than weakens the finding: nothing in the check ever compares against a real expected count.
- The local working `postgres` database currently holds zero public tables and zero product FKs to auth.users (only auth's own 8 internal FKs: identities, sessions, mfa_factors, oauth_authorizations, one_time_tokens, oauth_consents, webauthn_credentials, webauthn_challenges), so I could not reproduce against it and used a throwaway instead — which is the stronger evidence anyway since I controlled the exact FK count at each step.

SEVERITY: HIGH is right. The defect is in the one control whose stated purpose is to prevent vacuous passes, in the mode the runbook designates as the pre-restore/pre-cutover acceptance test, and the realistic trigger (partial auth.users restore, so only some FKs recreate) is the precise scenario the check was written for. No exploit path — it is a detector failure, as the finding itself states.

CONFIRMED by independent reproduction; not refuted.

Code: scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs:286-297 emits 'NO product foreign key references auth.users -- expected 10' only `where (select count(*) ... rn.nspname in ('public','app')) = 0`. Exact-zero threshold, message claims ten.

My own reproduction (I did NOT reuse the finder's probe2; the local `postgres` database currently has 0 base tables in public/app and 0 FKs to auth.users, so I built an isolated case): created throwaway db `refute_fk_opus`, made `auth.users` plus ten `public` tables each with an FK to it.
- count query -> 10; the check's exact SQL returned zero rows ([OK]).
- dropped 9 of 10 constraints; count query -> 1.
- `node scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs --check "postgresql://postgres:postgres@127.0.0.1:54322/refute_fk_opus"` printed literally `[OK] auth_user_foreign_keys_present` while nine of ten FKs were absent (other unrelated self-checks failed because the synthetic db lacks auth helpers/RLS, which does not affect this check's own verdict). Throwaway db dropped afterwards (DROP DATABASE confirmed).

ALREADY-MITIGATED lens, searched and came up empty for the `--check` path: no other SELF_CHECKS entry counts FKs (reviewed all nine, lines 252-430); no test asserts the ten FKs exist (grep for `confrelid` across tests/ hits nothing; only tests/integration/organizations-isolation.test.ts and scripts/perf/seed-p11-perf-setup.ts mention auth.users at all); `scripts/ops/` contains only this one script; grep shows no CI workflow invokes it. The one genuine compensating control is the TWO-database mode's `constraints` check (compare-database-posture.mjs:191-203), which compares `pg_get_constraintdef` for every constraint in public/app and would report nine missing FK rows as `[DIFFER] constraints -- CRITICAL`. But docs/runbooks/BACKUP_RESTORE.md:633 and docs/runbooks/DEPLOYMENT.md:574 both prescribe the single-database `--check` form as a gate on its own, and in that form the vacuous pass is real.

Severity corrected HIGH -> MEDIUM: it is a detector defect with no exploit path (the finding itself says so), and the documented source-vs-target acceptance test does catch the same loss. The realistic trigger the finding names is real and recorded in BACKUP_RESTORE.md Finding 3 (nine of ten `ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT` failures because auth.users is empty), and in that state a post-restore `--check` would print [OK] for this check. Fix is one character class: compare `< 10` (or assert per-table presence) instead of `= 0`.

title: `api_roles_hold_their_grants` also fires only at exactly zero: a database where `authenticated` holds one grant out of ~250 is certified POSTURE MATCHES
evidence:
scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs:382-400, predicate `... ) = 0`. Its own `why` (line 384) claims it 'catches a --no-privileges restore' and that without it 'the TRUNCATE check below passes vacuously on a database that has no grants at all -- which is exactly how a broken restore looks.' A near-total grant loss is not a no-grant loss.

On throwaway probe2:
  revoke all on all tables in schema public from authenticated, anon;
  grant select on public.countries to authenticated;
  grant select on public.countries to anon;

  select grantee, count(*) from information_schema.role_table_grants
   where table_schema='public' and grantee in ('anon','authenticated','service_role')
   group by grantee order by grantee;
  -> anon|1
  -> authenticated|1
  -> service_role|154

  node scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs --check <probe2>
  -> [OK] api_roles_hold_their_grants
  -> [OK] truncate_granted_to_api_roles
  -> RESULT: POSTURE MATCHES

For scale, BACKUP_RESTORE.md:544-552 measures the healthy figure as 506 of 506 API-role table grants.
exploit: NONE -- structural. The realistic trigger is a partial-privileges restore: a dump interrupted partway through its GRANT block, or a restore where only tables created before a certain point picked up their grants. `psql -f` without ON_ERROR_STOP continues past failures, which is the documented restore command shape.
impact: The gate that exists to prove privileges survived a restore proves only that they did not vanish entirely. A database in which the application is completely unusable -- no user can read a shipment or write an emission record -- passes every self-check, and passes it alongside `truncate_granted_to_api_roles`, which it exists to keep honest. Combined with finding 7 (nothing in the post-deploy gates exercises the database as a non-service role), such a database can be cut over to and reported healthy.
freshEnvironment: Yes -- a property of the script's SQL. Demonstrated on throwaway probe2, which was dropped afterwards.

verdicts.reasoning:
CONFIRMED as to mechanism; severity reduced from HIGH to MEDIUM because the primary documented restore gate does catch it.

1. Predicate confirmed by reading the source, not the finding's quote. scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs:383-400, the check `api_roles_hold_their_grants`, ends at line 394-397 with `and ( select count(*) from information_schema.role_table_grants g where g.table_schema = 'public' and g.grantee = r.rolname ) = 0`. Its `why` at line 384 is exactly as quoted, including the claim that without it "the TRUNCATE check below passes vacuously on a database that has no grants at all".

2. Runner semantics confirmed: lines 585-588, a SELF_CHECK is `[OK]` iff its query returns zero rows (`if (rows.length === 0) { console.log(\`[OK] ...\`); continue; }`). So "only fires at exactly zero" follows directly.

3. Re-ran the finding's experiment independently. The shared local `postgres` database's product schema is currently EMPTY (`select count(*) from information_schema.tables where table_schema='public'` -> `0`, and `supabase_migrations.schema_migrations` does not exist) — another session has it mid-reset — so I could not run the script end-to-end there. I created my own throwaway `refute_grants_op5`, put it in the partial-loss state, and ran the script's SQL verbatim:
   - state: `select grantee, count(*) ... group by grantee` -> `anon|1`, `authenticated|1`, `service_role|14`
   - `api_roles_hold_their_grants` SQL (copied verbatim from lines 386-398) -> 0 rows; `select count(*) from (<that sql>) s` -> `0`  => `[OK]`
   - `truncate_granted_to_api_roles` SQL (lines 405-411) -> 0 rows; count -> `0` => `[OK]`
   - then `revoke all on all tables in schema public from authenticated;` -> counts `anon|1`, `service_role|14` (authenticated absent), and the same SQL now returns `role authenticated holds only 0 grants in schema public -- privileges did not survive`.
   Threshold-at-exactly-zero is proven. Throwaway database dropped (`DROP DATABASE`, verified absent from `pg_database`).

4. Reachability check (the lens I was asked to apply). No other self-check in SELF_CHECKS (lines 252-430) inspects grants at all — the grant-comparing checks `effective_grants` (lines 123-135, critical) and `function_grants` (lines 169-181) exist ONLY in the two-DSN CHECKS list. So in `--check` mode nothing compensates. And `--check` alone IS a documented standalone gate: docs/runbooks/DEPLOYMENT.md:574 makes it step 6 of the rebuild-from-migrations recipe, and docs/runbooks/BACKUP_RESTORE.md:530 offers it "against a restored target on its own, before a source is available to compare with", with :633 telling the operator to run `--check` against the target. I also checked the surrounding gates and they do not compensate: app/api/health/route.ts builds its client from `src/infrastructure/supabase/client.ts`, which uses `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` (client.ts:79,86), so `check-product-schema` probes as service_role and is blind to anon/authenticated grant loss; scripts/smoke/production-smoke.mjs is documented STRICTLY READ-ONLY and "Nothing in this file signs in" (lines 5-8), its route list only asserting 307/302 redirects for signed-out users. So the finding's impact claim — such a database passes self-check, health and smoke — holds.

5. One supporting detail of the finding is WRONG and I am recording it. The finding says "`psql -f` without ON_ERROR_STOP continues past failures, which is the documented restore command shape." The documented restore command is BACKUP_RESTORE.md:283-285, which DOES pass `-v ON_ERROR_STOP=1`; only the informal prose at :504 says bare `psql -f`. The trigger story is not fully dead, because :600-606 records that the restore emits 12 `ERROR: permission denied to change default privileges` and that "a restore log with zero ERROR lines is not achievable from this artifact today" — so error-tolerant restores are the practical reality — and a dump truncated in its trailing ACL section leaves tables and data intact while losing grants, which is a genuine partial-loss shape. But the finding overstated its evidence here.

6. Why MEDIUM, not HIGH. BACKUP_RESTORE.md:520-533 states the restore acceptance test is the TWO-database compare, and that mode runs `effective_grants` (critical: true, lines 123-135), which compares the full grant multiset and would fail loudly on 1-of-506. The gap is confined to the secondary source-unavailable `--check` path. The consequence is also availability, not security: a database in this state breaks on the first request from any signed-in user rather than silently accepting bad data, unlike the 2026-09-03 missing-INSERT-policy defect this check was written for. Real gate weakness, correctly identified, narrower blast radius than claimed.

I tried to refute this three ways and failed on all three.

    where r.rolname in ('anon', 'authenticated', 'service_role')
      and (
        select count(*) from information_schema.role_table_grants g
        where g.table_schema = 'public' and g.grantee = r.rolname

The `why` string quoted from line 384 is also verbatim: "catches a --no-privileges restore. Without this, the TRUNCATE check below passes vacuously on a database that has no grants at all -- which is exactly how a broken restore looks". `= 0` fires only on total loss, not near-total loss.   BEFORE:            anon=21  authenticated=21  service_role=21
  after `revoke all on all tables in schema public from anon, authenticated;

  api_roles_hold_their_grants output: (empty) -> [OK]

A 95% grant loss passes both checks, and passes `truncate_granted_to_api_roles` — the check `api_roles_hold_their_grants` exists specifically to keep non-vacuous. That is precisely the finding's claim. Throwaway DB dropped afterwards; `select datname from pg_database` confirms `refute_grants_op5` is gone.

SUPPORTING, NOT REQUIRED: BACKUP_RESTORE.md:544-547 does measure the healthy figure as "506 of 506" API-role table grants and a `--no-privileges` restore as "154 of 506" — i.e. the project's own measured broken-restore case is NONZERO overall. (I could not determine the per-role distribution of those 154, so I do not claim the check fails to catch `--no-privileges`; if all 154 were service_role's, anon=0 and authenticated=0 and it would fire. That specific sub-claim is unproven either way and the finding does not depend on it.) BACKUP_RESTORE.md:163 does document "plain `psql -f`" as the restore method, supporting the partial-restore trigger.

There is no attacker path and the finding itself states exploit "NONE -- structural"; it requires an antecedent restore failure to matter at all. It is a real and correctly-described false-assurance gap in a certification gate — a completely unusable database is certified POSTURE MATCHES — which is why it is not LOW.

CONFIRMED by my own code read and my own live reproduction; I searched for a mitigation and found only a partial one.

1. Code. scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs:383-401 (`api_roles_hold_their_grants`) ends its WHERE with `) = 0` (line 400). It is a self-check, not a comparison, so it has no notion of an expected count. Its stated `why` (line 384) is "catches a --no-privileges restore. Without this, the TRUNCATE check below passes vacuously on a database that has no grants at all". A near-total loss is not a total loss, and the TRUNCATE check (lines 402-413) is a pure negative query, so it too passes vacuously at 1 grant.

2. Grant-reading SQL in the file, by line: 130 (`effective_grants`), 142-143 (`schema_usage_grants`), 175 (`function_grants`) are all inside `CHECKS` (const at line 52), which the runner executes ONLY in two-DSN mode (`if (!selfOnly)`, line 519). `SELF_CHECKS` begins at line 252; the only privilege-reading SQL inside it is lines 388/395 (the `= 0` predicate) and 406 (TRUNCATE). Every other self-check reads pg_policies / pg_class / pg_proc / pg_constraint / pg_namespace and is grant-independent, so a grant loss cannot make any of them fire.

title: Views are invisible to every check, and the schema's only view is the one object whose security is a reloption: `security_invoker=false` gives every authenticated user cross-org read of all calculation results, and the gate says POSTURE MATCHES
exploit: `GET /rest/v1/latest_calculation_results` with any valid authenticated JWT -- including one belonging to no organization at all -- returns every organization's calculation results: emissions figures, quantities, frozen determinations, engine versions and the user ids that produced them. The base table correctly returns nothing to the same session, which is what makes the loss silent.
impact: Cross-tenant disclosure of the platform's most commercially sensitive rows. A competitor's importer org would read another importer's per-line embedded emissions and quantities. The gate that certifies a restore cannot see it, and neither can the health check or the smoke script. I have not found a documented operation in this repo that strips the option (`pg_dump` does preserve `WITH (security_invoker='true')` -- probe_dump.sql:3532), so the finding is that the detector is blind, not that a specific procedure loses it: a hand-repaired view during recovery, a `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW` in a future migration that omits the clause, or a restore from an artifact predating 20260829200000 all land here undetected.
freshEnvironment: Yes. The blindness is a property of the script's SQL. The exploit itself was demonstrated on throwaway probe2 built by restoring the documented dump; probe2 was dropped afterwards and the working database's view still reads `reloptions=security_invoker=true`.

verdicts.reasoning:
I re-ran the finding's factual sub-claims and they hold, but the exploit is not reachable by any actor, which refutes it at HIGH.

WHAT I CONFIRMED (the true half):
1. The view ships with the option ON. supabase/migrations/20260829200000_p6_calculation_results_hardening.sql:80-81 `create view public.latest_calculation_results with (security_invoker = true)`. It is the only view in public (grep across supabase/ finds no other CREATE VIEW touching it, and no CREATE OR REPLACE of it in any later migration).
2. The posture script is blind to it. `grep -n "relkind\|BASE TABLE\|reloptions\|view\|VIEW\|security_invoker" scripts/ops/compare-database-posture.mjs` returns exactly 6 hits, all `relkind = 'r'` (lines 101, 272, 320, 333, 350) plus `table_type = 'BASE TABLE'` (line 73). Zero occurrences of `reloptions` or any view-aware query. Enumerating all 23 check names (`grep -n '    name: "'`) shows no view_definitions / reloptions / pg_get_viewdef check.
3. The mechanism is real. On a throwaway db (probe_view_op5, since dropped) with an RLS'd table + `security_invoker=true` view granted to authenticated:
   invoker_true  base=1 view=1
   invoker_false base=1 view=2   (real BEGIN/SET LOCAL ROLE authenticated/ROLLBACK)
   And `create or replace view public.v as select * from public.t;` (no WITH clause) silently resets the option: `after_cor_replace reloptions=NULL`. So a future migration that replaces the view without repeating the clause would indeed lose RLS undetected.

WHY IT IS REFUTED AS A HIGH SECURITY FINDING (reachability):
a. No actor can flip the option. In the same probe db: `set local role authenticated; alter view public.v set (security_invoker=false);` -> `ERROR: must be owner of view v`. The view is owner=postgres. anon/authenticated/service_role have no DDL on it. There is no dynamic SQL anywhere in the schema to smuggle DDL through: `grep -rn "execute format\|execute '" supabase/migrations/*.sql` returns nothing. So the "exploit" of `GET /rest/v1/latest_calculation_results` requires an operator with view ownership to first break the view by hand — it is not an exposure a real actor reaches.
b. The finding concedes there is no documented operation that strips the option, and I confirmed the one path it names is safe: `docker exec supabase_db_snowkap-cbam pg_dump -U postgres -d probe_view_op5 --schema=public` emits `CREATE VIEW public.v WITH (security_invoker='true') AS ...`. The restore path preserves it.
c. The "restore from an artifact predating 20260829200000" scenario is NOT undetected. information_schema.columns includes view columns (probe: `select table_name, count(*) from information_schema.columns where table_schema='public'` -> `v|3`, `t|3`), so an absent view drops its 17 column rows and the critical `columns` check (compare-database-posture.mjs:78-91) fails. That scenario is caught.
d. Unlike the seed.sql `grant all` class this review is hunting, nothing in ordinary operation (db reset, seed, restore, migration re-run, default privileges) touches a reloption. `alter default privileges` grants privileges, not storage options.

CAVEAT: I could not re-read the option on the working local database — its public schema is currently empty (`select nspname, count(*) ... group by 1` shows no `public` row at all; `supabase_migrations.schema_migrations` does not exist), i.e. another agent has wiped/is resetting it. I verified against the migration source and a purpose-built probe instead.

NET: this is a genuine coverage gap in a recovery-comparison script (worth adding a `reloptions`/view-definition check for, especially given (3)'s CREATE OR REPLACE hazard), not a cross-tenant disclosure in the release candidate. Downgraded HIGH -> LOW.

EXPLOIT REPRODUCED (throwaway db `refute_view_op5`, built by me, dropped afterwards). Table + RLS policy + the real view definition + seed.sql:19-22 blanket grants:

DETECTOR BLINDNESS PROVEN EMPIRICALLY: I ran the script's own SQL for `tables`, `rls_enabled`, `tables_without_rls`, `rls_without_policies`, `effective_grants` and `columns` against the secure and the fully-exploited state and diffed: 68 lines each, byte-identical, zero differences. The gate cannot see the difference between a locked-down view and a wide-open one.

WHERE I DISAGREE WITH THE FINDING — IT UNDERSTATES ITSELF: it says "I have not found a documented operation in this repo that strips the option." I found the ordinary one. `create or replace view public.latest_calculation_results as select ...` WITHOUT re-stating the WITH clause silently strips it: reloptions went `security_invoker=true` -> `-` (null), and the same no-org JWT immediately read `base_table=0 | view=26`. That is the standard idiom for amending a view, and this repo amends earlier objects constantly (74 migrations, chains up to `_v10`). So a future migration adding one column to this view, written the normal way, silently disables RLS on the platform's most sensitive rows while the release gate reports POSTURE MATCHES.

HIGH is justified: cross-tenant disclosure of per-line embedded emissions/quantities, on the single schema object whose security lives in a reloption no check reads, with a plausible ordinary path to losing it. Caveat kept for honesty: as the candidate ships today the option is present and pg_dump preserves it, so there is no live leak in the artifact — the defect is the blind gate plus the fragile idiom, not a currently-exploitable production hole.

title: This release's migrations are not additive, so the documented deploy order guarantees a calculate-feature outage and an application rollback to the recorded known-good SHA leaves it permanently broken -- a category ROLLBACK.md does not name
evidence:
supabase/migrations/20260903190000_p141_calculation_results_trusted_write_only.sql:144-148 does:
  drop policy if exists calculation_results_insert_own_org_as_self on public.calculation_results;
  revoke insert, update, delete on public.calculation_results from anon, authenticated;

The build currently serving production writes calculation results by direct table insert as the signed-in user. `git show a80e94c^:src/application/calculations/calculate-line.ts` line 240:
  .from("calculation_results")
  .insert(
 and its own comment at line 227 says 'calculation_results is writable by any authenticated member of the line's own org per its RLS policy'. The replacement port only exists on this branch (src/application/calculations/calculation-result-writer.ts).

The audit records 11 migrations pending against production (docs/plans/P14_FINAL_RELEASE_AUDIT.md:1514, :1086). DEPLOYMENT.md:517 is step 4 'Dry run, then push'; DEPLOYMENT.md:528 is step 6 'Only then deploy the application.' Between them, production runs the old code against the new schema.

ROLLBACK.md:159-170 defines the safe case as 'a new nullable column, a new table, a new index, a new RLS policy that doesn't remove a capability the old code relies on', and ROLLBACK.md:171 defines destructive as '(dropped or renamed a column/table the old code reads or writes, tightened a constraint the old code's writes would now violate)'. A dropped RLS policy and a revoked table grant appear in neither list. ROLLBACK.md:73-90 then instructs the operator to roll back to the SHA that was healthy before the release -- which is exactly the build that cannot write a calculation result once 20260903190000 has applied.
exploit:
1. Follow DEPLOYMENT.md step 4: `supabase db push` promotes all 11 pending migrations, including 20260903190000.
2. Before step 6 completes, any importer member clicks Calculate. The old deployed code issues `insert into calculation_results` as `authenticated`; the grant is gone and the policy is gone, so it fails.
3. If anything then goes wrong and ROLLBACK.md §1 is followed to the recorded known-good SHA, the same failure becomes permanent: the schema cannot be rolled back (ROLLBACK.md:150, forward-only), and the old code has no service-role path to `record_calculation_result`.
impact: A guaranteed outage window on the platform's core workflow during every promotion of this release, and a rollback procedure that -- followed exactly as written, including its own 'record the known-good SHA before the release deploy' instruction -- lands the operator in a state where calculating emissions is broken and the runbook offers no compensating step. The failure is silent to every gate: /api/health, /status and production-smoke.mjs all stay green (see finding 7). The condition is real for the very next production change, not hypothetical.
freshEnvironment: Yes -- this is a property of the migration set and the two runbooks, not of any database instance. Verified by reading the migration file, the pre-P14.1 application source out of git (`git show a80e94c^:...`), and the runbook line numbers cited. I did not touch production.

verdicts.reasoning:
Mechanism confirmed, conclusion refuted. Confirmed: 20260903190000_p141_calculation_results_trusted_write_only.sql:144-148 drops calculation_results_insert_own_org_as_self and revokes insert/update/delete from anon, authenticated; `git show 95c95bb:src/application/calculations/calculate-line.ts` lines 240-241 do `.from("calculation_results").insert(` on the client supplied by app/(importer)/shipments/[id]/actions.ts, which is getServerSupabaseClient() (the RLS `authenticated` client); DEPLOYMENT.md:517 (push) precedes :528 (deploy app); P14_FINAL_RELEASE_AUDIT.md:263 records production on 95c95bb with 11 pending migrations.

The finding's load-bearing claim is false, and refuted by a line it quotes itself. ROLLBACK.md:160-163 defines the SAFE branch as additive changes including "a new RLS policy that doesn't remove a capability the old code relies on" — capability removal is the doc's own discriminator, so a dropped policy plus a revoked grant is inside the destructive branch by definition, not "a category ROLLBACK.md does not name." The finding then stops quoting at :173 and omits ROLLBACK.md:180-183, which is the compensating step and is category-general: "Before rolling back application code past a destructive migration, explicitly confirm the target commit's code is still compatible with the *current* schema, not the schema as it existed when that commit was written." ROLLBACK.md:184-196 additionally prescribes a new forward corrective migration as the remedy for a bad applied migration, so "permanently broken" is also wrong — a re-grant migration, or rolling forward, resolves it.

Reachability of the residual step-4→step-6 window fails as well: it needs a signed-in importer member to click Calculate inside a window DEPLOYMENT.md:521 requires be "one contiguous window, with someone watching"; production is recorded as a "pre-release deployment with no real users" (P13_RELEASE_READINESS_REPORT.md:4020) holding 1 shipment line total (:4022-4026); and DEPLOYMENT.md:484-489 already states the general hazard ("'The migration is inert until the code lands' is not true in general and must never be assumed"). No real actor is positioned to experience the outage.

Live re-run of a DB probe was not possible: the local postgres database has been emptied by another session — `select count(*) from pg_tables where schemaname='public'` returned `0`, and `select count(*) from supabase_migrations.schema_migrations` returned `ERROR: relation "supabase_migrations.schema_migrations" does not exist`. Grant semantics are not in dispute and the refutation rests on file contents, not DB state.

Residual worth at most a doc nit: ROLLBACK.md:171-173's parenthetical examples of "destructive" ("dropped or renamed a column/table…, tightened a constraint…") could also name revoked grants and dropped policies, so an operator reading the parenthetical as exhaustive is not mis-served by the surrounding text but could be by the list.

I re-ran every piece of the finding's evidence independently; the technical core is correct.

1) The migration is non-additive, exactly as quoted. supabase/migrations/20260903190000_p141_calculation_results_trusted_write_only.sql:144-148 reads verbatim:
  drop policy if exists calculation_results_insert_own_org_as_self
      on public.calculation_results;
  revoke insert, update, delete on public.calculation_results
      from anon, authenticated;
And the replacement channel is service_role-only — lines 353-359:
  revoke all on function public.record_calculation_result(...) from public, anon, authenticated;
  grant execute on function public.record_calculation_result(...) to service_role;
(The file's own header at :90-92 states the same: "This one is granted to `service_role` ONLY.")

2) The build production actually serves does write by direct table INSERT as the signed-in user. I did not take `a80e94c^` on trust — I went to the deploy branch named by DEPLOYMENT.md. `git log --oneline -1 origin/feature/full-product-build` = 95c95bb ("docs(p13): CI integration gate green -- run 33637049603 on the deploy branch"). On that branch:
  git show origin/feature/full-product-build:src/application/calculations/calculate-line.ts | grep -n 'from("calculation_results")'  ->  240:      .from("calculation_results")
  git cat-file -e origin/feature/full-product-build:src/application/calculations/calculation-result-writer.ts  ->  "exists on disk, but not in 'origin/feature/full-product-build'" (the RPC port is branch-only, as claimed)
  git diff --stat origin/feature/full-product-build a80e94c^ -- src/application/calculations/calculate-line.ts  ->  no diff for that file, so the finding's `a80e94c^` quote is the deployed file.
The client is the user-scoped one, not admin: git show "origin/feature/full-product-build:app/(importer)/shipments/[id]/actions.ts" shows calculateLineAction obtaining `getServerSupabaseClient()` (line 1011 in that file) and passing it to calculateLine — role `authenticated`, so the revoked grant is exactly the one it uses. The old code has no service_role path and never calls record_calculation_result at all.

3) The deploy order is as cited. grep -n on docs/runbooks/DEPLOYMENT.md: 517 = "4. **Dry run, then push.** `supabase db push --dry-run`..."; 528 = "6. **Only then deploy the application.**", with step 5 (a read-only probe pass) in between. Nothing in that procedure defers or app-orders a capability-removing migration; its preamble warns the opposite way only ("The migration is inert until the code lands" is not true in general). grep -rn "20260903190000" docs/ --include=*.md returns six hits, none of which discusses deploy ordering or the old build's incompatibility.

4) The migration is genuinely pending against production: docs/plans/P14_FINAL_RELEASE_AUDIT.md:1887 "| Pending | **11** — `20260902150000`, `20260903100000`…`20260903190000` |" and :1514 "Migration ledger | 63 applied both sides, **11 pending**, no drift".

I could not do a live grant probe: the local cluster at 127.0.0.1:54322 is currently empty (select count(*) from pg_tables where tablename='calculation_results' -> 0; supabase_migrations.schema_migrations does not exist), so another agent has it mid-reset. That does not affect the conclusion — the claim is a property of the migration file plus the deployed source, both of which I read directly, and the audit itself records at :2301 that this migration's revoke did take effect locally ("INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on `calculation_results` revoked | `20260903190000` | handed all three back").

WHERE THE FINDING IS WRONG (why I lower the severity): its claim that this is "a category ROLLBACK.md does not name" and that "the runbook offers no compensating step" is inaccurate. ROLLBACK.md:163 defines the additive-safe case as "a new RLS policy that doesn't remove a capability the old code relies on" — a qualifier that excludes this migration precisely, so the runbook does classify it as not-safe. And ROLLBACK.md:181 supplies the compensating instruction the finding says is absent: "Before rolling back application code past a destructive migration, explicitly confirm the target commit's code is still compatible with the *current* schema, not the schema as it existed when that commit was written." The gap is narrower than claimed: the destructive-examples parenthetical (dropped/renamed column or table, tightened constraint) does not literally enumerate a revoked grant or dropped policy, so an operator classifying by the examples rather than by the qualifier could misfile it as additive — a real but documentation-shaped weakness, not the absence of any compensating step.

Net: the guaranteed outage window between DEPLOYMENT.md steps 4 and 6, and the fact that a rollback to the pre-release SHA leaves calculate permanently broken (forward-only schema per ROLLBACK.md §2, no service_role path in the old code), are both confirmed. MEDIUM rather than HIGH: no security or data-integrity impact, the window is operator-supervised and minutes long, the failure is a rejected write rather than a corrupt one, and ROLLBACK.md already carries the check that catches the rollback trap.

Confirmed by my own reading of every cited artifact; I could not refute it, but the claimed severity is too high.
